# HTTP.jl documentation

> Complete documentation for HTTP.jl v2.11.1 in one markdown file: every page of https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/ in reading order, with all docstrings expanded. The short page index is at https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/llms.txt.

---

<!-- Page: https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/ -->

# HTTP.jl

HTTP.jl is an HTTP client and server library for Julia. It speaks HTTP/1.1 and
HTTP/2, streams request and response bodies, and supports WebSockets and
server-sent events. [Reseau](https://github.com/JuliaServices/Reseau.jl)
provides the TCP, DNS, and TLS layers.

## Quick Start

Start a server, send it a request, and read the response body:

```julia
using HTTP

server = HTTP.serve!("127.0.0.1", 0) do req
    return HTTP.Response(200; body = "hello from HTTP.jl")
end

resp = HTTP.get("http://127.0.0.1:$(HTTP.port(server))/hello")
HTTP.forceclose(server)
String(resp.body)  # "hello from HTTP.jl"
```

Port `0` asks the operating system for a free port; `HTTP.port(server)`
returns the one it chose.

## Where to Go Next

- The [Client guide](https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/guides/client/) covers requests, streaming, reusable
  clients, request bodies, retries, and timeouts.
- The [Server guide](https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/guides/server/) covers request and stream handlers,
  routing, static files, server-sent events, and server timeouts.
- The [Protocols guide](https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/guides/protocols/) covers WebSockets and HTTP/2.
- The [Migration guide](https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/guides/migration-1x/) explains how to update code
  written for HTTP.jl 1.x.
- The [API reference](https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/api/reference/) lists every public name with its
  docstring.

Give either file to an assistant when you ask it about HTTP.jl.

# Client Guide

`HTTP.request` and the verb helpers such as `HTTP.get` and `HTTP.post` send a
request and return an `HTTP.Response` with the whole body in memory.
`HTTP.open` streams the response instead. An `HTTP.Client` holds
connections and settings that you want to share across requests.

## Making Requests

```julia
using HTTP

server = HTTP.serve!("127.0.0.1", 0) do req
    return HTTP.Response(200; body = "$(req.method) $(req.target)")
end
url = "http://127.0.0.1:$(HTTP.port(server))"

resp = HTTP.request("GET", url * "/hello")
resp.status        # 200
String(resp.body)  # "GET /hello"

HTTP.forceclose(server)
```

`HTTP.get`, `HTTP.head`, `HTTP.post`, `HTTP.put`, `HTTP.patch`, `HTTP.delete`,
`HTTP.options`, and `HTTP.query` call `HTTP.request` with a fixed method and
accept the same keywords.

A response with status 300 or above throws an `HTTP.StatusError`.
Redirect responses (301, 302, 303, 307, and 308) are the exception. Pass
`status_exception = false` to get the response instead.

The client follows up to 10 redirects. Set `redirect = false` or
`redirect_limit` to change that. A `Location` header is resolved against the
current URL as [RFC 3986](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986#section-5.2)
specifies: `.` and `..` segments are removed, while repeated slashes and
percent-encoded bytes are kept. The path of the URL you pass is sent as written,
and fragments are never sent.

## Request Bodies

Pass the body as the third positional argument or with the `body` keyword.
Strings and byte vectors are sent as they are. Files and `IOBuffer`s are read
into memory first. Other `IO` values, and iterables of strings or byte chunks,
are streamed with chunked transfer encoding.

HTTP.jl has no JSON dependency. Serialize the payload yourself, for example with
[JSON.jl](https://github.com/JuliaIO/JSON.jl), and set the `Content-Type`
header:

```julia
using HTTP, JSON

resp = HTTP.post(
    "https://api.example.com/users";
    headers = ["Content-Type" => "application/json"],
    body = JSON.json(Dict("name" => "alice", "age" => 30)),
)
user = JSON.parse(String(resp.body))
```

A `Dict` or `NamedTuple` body is sent as an HTML form
(`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`), and the `Content-Type` header is set for
you:

```julia
HTTP.post("https://example.com/login", [], Dict("user" => "alice", "pw" => "s3cret"))
```

Use `HTTP.Form` for `multipart/form-data`, such as file uploads. An open
file is sent with its file name:

```julia
open("upload.bin") do file
    HTTP.post("https://example.com/upload", [], HTTP.Form(Dict("file" => file, "kind" => "binary")))
end
```

### QUERY requests

[RFC 10008](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc10008) defines the `QUERY` method
for safe, idempotent requests that carry a body. `HTTP.query` sends one:

```julia
HTTP.query(
    "https://api.example.com/search";
    headers = ["Content-Type" => "application/json"],
    body = """{"select":["name","email"],"limit":10}""",
)
```

## Query Parameters

The `query` keyword URL-encodes a `Dict`, `NamedTuple`, or vector of pairs and
appends it to the URL's query string:

```julia
HTTP.get("https://example.com/search"; query = Dict("page" => 2, "limit" => 10))
# GET /search?limit=10&page=2
```

A `Dict` has no order. Use a vector of pairs to fix the order or to repeat a key:

```julia
HTTP.get("https://example.com/search"; query = ["tag" => "a", "tag" => "b"])
# GET /search?tag=a&tag=b
```

`query` adds to a query string that is already in the URL:

```julia
HTTP.get("https://example.com/search?type=user"; query = ["page" => 2])
# GET /search?type=user&page=2
```

## Reading the Response Body

`resp.body` is a `Vector{UInt8}`. Convert it to text with `String`:

```julia
resp = HTTP.get("https://example.com")
text = String(resp.body)
```

!!! warning "`String(resp.body)` empties `resp.body`"
    `String(::Vector{UInt8})` takes over the vector's memory instead of copying
    it, so `resp.body` is empty afterwards. Use `String(copy(resp.body))` if you
    need the bytes again.

## Streaming Responses

`HTTP.open` sends the request and lets you read the response body as it
arrives. It follows redirects and decompresses the body like `HTTP.request`.

```julia
resp = HTTP.open("GET", "https://example.com") do stream
    while !eof(stream)
        chunk = readavailable(stream)
        # process chunk
    end
end
```

The `do` block form returns the final `HTTP.Response`, not the value of the
block. Store anything you need from the block in a variable defined outside it.
Call `HTTP.startread(stream)` inside the block to see the status and headers
before you read the body.

To copy the body into an `IO` instead, pass it as `response_stream`. The
response's `body` is then `nothing`:

```julia
buf = IOBuffer()
resp = HTTP.get("https://example.com"; response_stream = buf)
text = String(take!(buf))
```

## Reusing a Client

Calls without a `client` keyword share one default client, so they already reuse
connections and share a cookie jar. Create your own `HTTP.Client` when a
set of requests needs its own connection pool, cookies, or settings:

```julia
client = HTTP.Client(
    transport = HTTP.Transport(max_idle_per_host = 4),
    cookiejar = HTTP.CookieJar(),
)
resp = HTTP.get(client, "https://example.com")
close(client)
```

Every request function accepts the client as its first argument or as the
`client` keyword. A closed client throws `ArgumentError` when you use it;
`isopen(client)` tells you whether it is still open.

Settings are split between the two types:

- `HTTP.Transport` owns connections: pool sizes (`max_idle_per_host`,
  `max_idle_total`, `max_conns_per_host`), `idle_timeout_ns`, TLS settings
  (`tls_config`), the proxy (`proxy`), the retry budget (`retry_bucket`), the
  source address (`local_addr`), and the response header limits
  (`max_line_bytes` and `max_header_bytes`).
- `HTTP.Client` owns request policy: the transport, the cookie jar,
  redirects (`max_redirects`, `check_redirect`), HTTP/2 (`prefer_http2`,
  `http2_settings`), and per-request defaults.

A `Client` created without a `transport` reads its proxy from the
`HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY`, and `NO_PROXY` environment variables
when it is created. A `Transport` you create yourself connects directly unless
you pass `proxy`.
Proxy URLs may use `http://`, `socks5://`, or `socks5h://`.

### Per-client defaults

A client can carry defaults that apply to every request sent through it:

```julia
client = HTTP.Client(
    default_headers = ["User-Agent" => "MyApp/1.0", "X-API-Version" => "v2"],
    default_query = Dict("api_key" => "secret"),
    default_basicauth = "alice" => "password",
    connect_timeout = 5,
    request_timeout = 30,
)

HTTP.get(client, "https://api.example.com/users")

# Per-call values replace the defaults they overlap.
HTTP.get(client, "https://api.example.com/users"; headers = ["X-API-Version" => "v1"])
```

- `default_headers` are added unless the call sets the same header.
- `default_query` is merged with the call's `query`; keys in the call replace
  the default values for the same key.
- `default_basicauth` is used unless the call passes `basicauth` or an
  `Authorization` header.
- The timeouts (`connect_timeout`, `request_timeout`, `response_header_timeout`,
  `read_idle_timeout`, `write_idle_timeout`) apply when the call passes no value
  or `0`.

### Binding to a local address

`local_addr` sets the source IP address of a client's connections, which picks
the outgoing interface on a host with several. Pass an IP address string, or a
`Reseau.TCP.SocketAddrV4` or `SocketAddrV6` to also fix the source port:

```julia
client = HTTP.Client(local_addr = "192.0.2.10")
```

The address must belong to a local interface. Interface names such as `"en0"`
throw an `ArgumentError`. When you pass your own `transport`, set `local_addr` on
the `Transport` instead.

## Timeouts

Each timeout keyword bounds one part of a request. All values are in seconds.

- `connect_timeout` bounds DNS lookup, the TCP connect, the proxy `CONNECT` or
  SOCKS5 handshake, the TLS handshake, and HTTP/2 connection setup. It
  defaults to 30.
- `request_timeout` bounds the whole call.
- `response_header_timeout` bounds the wait for the response headers after the
  request is sent.
- `read_idle_timeout` bounds the time between reads, including the wait for the
  response headers.
- `write_idle_timeout` bounds the time between writes.
- `expect_continue_timeout` sets how long an HTTP/1 upload with an
  `Expect: 100-continue` header waits for `100 Continue` before it sends the
  body anyway.

`request_timeout`, `response_header_timeout`, `read_idle_timeout`, and
`write_idle_timeout` are off unless you set them. A timeout throws
`HTTP.TimeoutError`.

```julia
resp = HTTP.get(
    "https://example.com";
    connect_timeout = 2,
    response_header_timeout = 5,
    read_idle_timeout = 30,
)
```

`HTTP.open` takes the same keywords. `HTTP.WebSockets.open` takes all of them
except `expect_continue_timeout`.

## Retries

By default a request is retried up to 4 times (`retries = 4`) when all of these
hold:

- the method is `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`, `QUERY`, `PUT`, or `DELETE`,
  or the request has an `Idempotency-Key` or `X-Idempotency-Key` header (pass
  `retry_non_idempotent = true` to retry other requests)
- the body can be sent again, which is true unless it is streamed from an `IO`
  or an iterable
- the attempt failed with a network error, such as a refused or reset
  connection, or the response status is 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, or 504

Retries wait a random, exponentially growing delay, or the delay that a 429 or
503 response asks for in its `Retry-After` header, up to 20 seconds. Pass
`retry = false` to turn retries off. Each `Transport` also has a
`HTTP.RetryBucket` that limits how many retries a burst of failures can
trigger.

Pass `retry_if` to make your own decision:

```julia
function retry_if(attempt, err, req, resp)
    err !== nothing && return attempt <= 2      # failed before a response
    return resp.status in (429, 503) && attempt <= 3
end

HTTP.get("https://example.com"; retry_if = retry_if)
```

`retry_if(attempt, err, req, resp)` gets the one-based number of the attempt
that just finished. For a failure before any response, `err` is an
`HTTP.RequestRetryError` whose `err.err` field holds the underlying
exception, and `resp` is `nothing`. For a response, `err` is `nothing` and `resp`
is the response. Return `true` to retry, `false` to stop, or `nothing` to use the
default rules. A body that cannot be sent again is never retried.

## Cancellation and Deadlines

Pass an `HTTP.RequestContext` as `context` to control a request from
another task. `HTTP.cancel!(ctx)` aborts the request, which then throws
`HTTP.CanceledError`:

```julia
ctx = HTTP.RequestContext()
task = Threads.@spawn HTTP.get("https://example.com/slow"; context = ctx)
HTTP.cancel!(ctx)
fetch(task)  # throws a TaskFailedException wrapping an HTTP.CanceledError
```

A context can also carry an absolute deadline, set with
`HTTP.RequestContext(deadline_ns = time_ns() + 5_000_000_000)` or
`HTTP.set_deadline!`. A request still running at the deadline throws
`HTTP.TimeoutError`. `HTTP.request`, the verb helpers, `HTTP.open`, and
`HTTP.do!` all accept `context`.

## Debugging Requests

`verbose = 1` prints a line for each attempt, response, retry, and redirect,
and one for the result. `verbose = 2` also prints the request and response
heads:

```julia
HTTP.get("http://127.0.0.1:8080/v"; verbose = 2)
```

```
[http] request attempt 1 GET http://127.0.0.1:8080/v via h1
[http] request
GET /v HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:8080
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate
User-Agent: HTTP.jl/2.0.0
[http] response attempt 1 200 for http://127.0.0.1:8080/v
[http] response
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 6
[http] done 200 for http://127.0.0.1:8080/v
```

To collect the same information in code, pass a `trace` callback. It receives
these events: `HTTP.RequestEvent`, `HTTP.ResponseHeadEvent`,
`HTTP.RetryEvent`, `HTTP.RetrySkippedEvent`,
`HTTP.RedirectEvent`, and `HTTP.DoneEvent`.

## Avoiding Copies

A byte vector or contiguous byte view passed as the body is sent without being
copied, and retries send the same bytes again. Do not change the bytes until the
call returns.

Pass `copyheaders = false` with an `HTTP.Headers` collection to let
`HTTP.request` or `HTTP.open` use it without copying it first. Do not touch the
collection until the call returns, and do not share it between requests that run
at the same time; its contents afterwards are unspecified. Other header inputs
are always copied.

```julia
payload = read("upload.bin")
headers = HTTP.Headers(["Content-Type" => "application/octet-stream"])
resp = HTTP.put("https://example.com/upload", headers, payload; copyheaders = false)
```

A byte vector or writable byte view passed as `response_stream` receives the
body directly. It must be large enough for the whole body, or the call throws
`ArgumentError`. A `Vector{UInt8}` is resized to the body length. A response
with status 300 or above, including a redirect that is not followed, leaves it
untouched: up to 1 MiB of that body is returned in `resp.body` instead, so a
`StatusError` still carries it.

---

<!-- Page: https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/guides/server/ -->

# Server Guide

`HTTP.serve!` calls your function with each `HTTP.Request` and sends
the `HTTP.Response` it returns. `HTTP.listen!` calls your function with
an `HTTP.Stream` instead, so it can read the request body and write the
response in pieces. Both return an `HTTP.Server` right away; `HTTP.serve`
and `HTTP.listen` take the same arguments and block until the server closes.

## Request Handlers

```julia
using HTTP

server = HTTP.serve!("127.0.0.1", 8080) do req
    return HTTP.Response(200; headers = ["Content-Type" => "text/plain"], body = "handled " * req.target)
end

resp = HTTP.get("http://127.0.0.1:8080/health")
String(resp.body)  # "handled /health"
HTTP.forceclose(server)
```

A handler that throws sends the client a `500 Internal Server Error`.

### Reading the request

`req.method` and `req.target` hold the request line, and `HTTP.header(req,
"Content-Type")` reads a header. `String(req.body)` returns the body as text.

`req.target` holds the path and the query string. Split them with `HTTP.URI`
and decode the query with `HTTP.queryparams`, which returns a `Dict`, or
`HTTP.queryparampairs`, which keeps the order and repeated keys. A form body
(`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) uses the same encoding, so
`HTTP.queryparams` decodes it too:

```julia
HTTP.serve!("127.0.0.1", 8080) do req
    query = HTTP.queryparams(HTTP.URI(req.target).query)
    form = HTTP.queryparams(String(req.body))
    return HTTP.Response(200; body = "page $(get(query, "page", "1")), user $(get(form, "user", "?"))")
end
```

Use `HTTP.parse_multipart_form` for a `multipart/form-data` body.

`serve!` reads the whole request body into memory before it calls the handler.
`max_body_bytes` limits the size, 64 MiB by default; a larger body gets
`413 Content Too Large`. Pass `max_body_bytes = 0` for no limit, or use a
stream handler to read large bodies in pieces.

### Reusing responses

A `Response` with a `String` or `Vector{UInt8}` body is not used up when it is
sent, so a handler can return the same response object every time:

```julia
const HEALTH = HTTP.Response(200; headers = ["Content-Type" => "text/plain"], body = "ok")
handler(req) = HEALTH
```

A streamed body, such as an `HTTP.CallbackBody`, can be sent only once.
Sending it again gives the client a `500 Internal Server Error`.

## Stream Handlers

A stream handler reads the request and writes the response itself:

```julia
server = HTTP.listen!("127.0.0.1", 8080) do stream
    req = HTTP.startread(stream)  # the request line and headers
    body = read(stream)           # the request body
    HTTP.setstatus(stream, 200)
    HTTP.setheader(stream, "Content-Type" => "text/plain")
    write(stream, "got $(length(body)) bytes for $(req.target)")
end
```

Set the status and headers before the first `write`. A response without a
`Content-Length` header is sent with chunked encoding, and
`HTTP.addtrailer` adds trailers to it. `HTTP.streamhandler(f)` turns a
request handler `f` into a stream handler.

### Fixed-length responses

A stream handler that sets `Content-Length` on an HTTP/1 response and writes
without calling `HTTP.startwrite` has its body held in memory until it
returns or calls `closewrite`. Until then nothing is sent, so if the handler
throws or writes the wrong number of bytes, the client gets an error response
instead.

To stream a large body, call `HTTP.startwrite` first. The server still holds
the first 4 KiB, so a small response goes out in one write with its head. Once
the body passes 4 KiB, the head and the held bytes are sent, and each later
`write` goes straight to the connection:

```julia
HTTP.listen!("127.0.0.1", 8080) do stream
    HTTP.setheader(stream, "Content-Length" => string(filesize(path)))
    HTTP.startwrite(stream)
    open(io -> write(stream, io), path)
end
```

Once the head is sent, a failure can only close the connection. Either way,
writing more than `Content-Length` bytes throws. `HTTP.streamhandler` streams
a response body this way when it is not already in memory, such as a
`fileserver` file.

## Interactive Thread Pool

HTTP.jl runs its server tasks, including your handlers, on Julia's
`:interactive` thread pool. That keeps the server answering requests, health
checks included, while compute-heavy tasks keep the `:default` pool busy.

Start a production server with at least one interactive thread. This command
starts four default threads and one interactive thread:

```sh
julia --threads=4,1 --project=. server.jl
```

`JULIA_NUM_THREADS=4,1` does the same. Without an interactive thread, Julia runs
these tasks on the default pool, where tasks that never yield can stall the
server.

Do not run long computations directly in a handler: they hold an interactive
thread. Run them on the default pool and wait for the result:

```julia
result = fetch(Threads.@spawn :default expensive_work())
```

## Server Lifecycle

Keep the `Server` that `serve!` or `listen!` returns:

- `HTTP.port(server)` returns the bound port, which is useful with port `0`.
- `wait(server)` blocks until the server stops accepting connections.
- `close(server)` stops accepting connections and waits for the requests in
  progress to finish.
- `HTTP.forceclose(server)` stops at once and closes every connection.

### Timeouts

All server timeouts are off by default. Each keyword takes seconds, and a
variant ending in `_ns`, such as `read_timeout_ns`, takes nanoseconds:

```julia
server = HTTP.serve!(
    handler,
    "127.0.0.1",
    8080;
    read_header_timeout = 5,
    read_timeout = 30,
    write_timeout = 30,
    idle_timeout = 120,
)
```

For HTTP/1 connections, `read_header_timeout` limits reading the request line
and headers. After the headers, `read_timeout` starts a fresh limit for reading
the body. Between requests on a kept-alive connection, `idle_timeout` applies
until the next request starts to arrive; the header limit starts then. When the
header or idle setting is `0`, it falls back to `read_timeout`.

When a header or body read times out, the server answers
`408 Request Timeout` and closes the connection. An idle timeout closes the
connection without a response.

### TLS

To serve HTTPS, pass `serve!` or `listen!` a TLS listener from Reseau. List
`"h2"` in `alpn_protocols` to offer HTTP/2 to clients:

```julia
using HTTP, Reseau

config = Reseau.TLS.Config(;
    cert_file = "cert.pem",
    key_file = "key.pem",
    alpn_protocols = ["h2", "http/1.1"],
)
server = HTTP.serve!(handler, Reseau.TLS.listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:8443", config))
```

See the [Protocols guide](https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/guides/protocols/) for HTTP/2 on plain connections.

## Routing and Middleware

`HTTP.Router` matches a request's method and path
against registered routes:

```julia
using HTTP

router = HTTP.Router()

HTTP.register!(router, "GET", "/users/{id}") do req
    id = HTTP.getparam(req, "id")
    return HTTP.Response(200; body = "user " * id)
end

server = HTTP.serve!(router, "127.0.0.1", 8080)
```

Read the matched route and its path variables with `HTTP.getroute`,
`HTTP.getparams`, and `HTTP.getparam`. A path that matches no route gets
`404 Not Found`, and a path that matches with another method gets
`405 Method Not Allowed`.

Middleware is a function that takes a handler and returns a new handler. The
third argument of `Router` wraps every route registered on it. This router
gives each handler 5 seconds:

```julia
timeout = HTTP.Handlers.handlertimeout(5.0; status = 503)
router = HTTP.Router(
    req -> HTTP.Response(404),
    req -> HTTP.Response(405),
    timeout,
)
```

### Request logging

`HTTP.Handlers.logging_middleware` wraps a handler and logs one record per
request through Julia's logging system:

```julia
using HTTP, Logging

server = HTTP.serve!(HTTP.Handlers.logging_middleware(router), "127.0.0.1", 8080)
```

With the default `ConsoleLogger`, each request prints a record like:

```
┌ Info: GET /users/42 200 0.412ms
│   method = "GET"
│   target = "/users/42"
│   status = 200
│   elapsed_ms = 0.412
└   length = 7
```

`length` is the response body length when it is known without reading the
body. A handler that throws is logged at `Logging.Error` with the exception,
which is then rethrown, so the client still gets an error response. Pass
`level` to log successful requests at another level, and `logger` to send the
records to a specific logger:

```julia
access_log = HTTP.Handlers.logging_middleware(router; level = Logging.Debug)
```

The middleware also wraps stream handlers; their records add the client's
`peer` address. Every record is in the `:access` log group, so it is easy to
filter or route with a package such as LoggingExtras.jl.

## Static Files

`HTTP.fileserver(root)` returns a request handler that serves the files under
the directory `root`:

```julia
using HTTP

handler = HTTP.fileserver("public"; spa_fallback = "index.html")
server = HTTP.serve!(handler, "127.0.0.1", 8080)
```

It serves `index.html` for a directory and redirects to the canonical path of a
file or directory. `spa_fallback` serves the given file for a missing path that
does not look like a file name, as a single-page app needs. It answers
`If-Modified-Since` and single `Range` requests, and also `If-None-Match` when
you pass `etag`.

`HTTP.servefile` serves one file for a request, and
`HTTP.servecontent` serves bytes or a seekable `IO` that you already
have, with the same conditional and range handling. For a string, pass
`codeunits(str)`.

## Server-Sent Events

`HTTP.sse_stream` builds a `text/event-stream` response. Write
`HTTP.SSEEvent` values in its `do` block, which runs on its own task;
the stream ends when the block returns:

```julia
using HTTP

server = HTTP.serve!("127.0.0.1", 8080) do req
    return HTTP.sse_stream(200) do stream
        write(stream, HTTP.SSEEvent("ready"; event = "status", id = "1"))
    end
end
```

A client reads the events with the `sse_callback` keyword of `HTTP.request`.

## HTTP/2

`serve!` and `listen!` speak HTTP/2 to clients that ask for it, through TLS
(see [TLS](#TLS)) or cleartext prior knowledge. The [Protocols
guide](https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/guides/protocols/#HTTP/2) covers the details and the `http2_settings`
keyword.

---

<!-- Page: https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/guides/protocols/ -->

# Protocols Guide

This page covers WebSockets and HTTP/2. HTTP/2 needs no separate API: the
client and server functions from the other guides use it when both sides
support it.

## WebSockets

The WebSocket API lives in the `HTTP.WebSockets` submodule. `using HTTP` also
exports the name `WebSockets`; these docs write `HTTP.WebSockets` so that
another package's `WebSockets` cannot shadow it.

`HTTP.WebSockets.listen!` starts a server that calls your function with each
new connection. `HTTP.WebSockets.open` connects to a `ws://` or `wss://` URL:

```julia
using HTTP

server = HTTP.WebSockets.listen!("127.0.0.1", 0) do ws
    for msg in ws
        HTTP.WebSockets.send(ws, uppercase(msg))
    end
end

url = "ws://" * HTTP.WebSockets.server_addr(server)
reply = HTTP.WebSockets.open(url) do ws
    HTTP.WebSockets.send(ws, "hello")
    HTTP.WebSockets.receive(ws)
end
HTTP.WebSockets.forceclose(server)
reply  # "HELLO"
```

Iterating over a WebSocket yields each message until the peer closes the
connection. `receive` returns a `String` for a text message and a
`Vector{UInt8}` for a binary one. The `do` block form of `open` returns the
block's value and closes the connection when the block ends.

To serve WebSockets and ordinary HTTP routes from one server, upgrade requests
by hand inside an `HTTP.listen!` handler; see `HTTP.WebSockets.upgrade`.

`HTTP.WebSockets.open` also accepts an `IO` that is already connected, such as a
`TCPSocket` or a TLS stream, instead of a URL. Pass the request `target` and
`host` as keywords. `open` never closes that `IO`:

```julia
ws = HTTP.WebSockets.open(io; target = "/echo", host = "example.com")
```

### Limits and timeouts

`maxframesize` limits the size of one incoming frame, and `maxfragmentation`
the number of frames in one message. They default to 16 MiB and 1024 on clients
and servers; pass larger values if your protocol needs them. A peer that goes
over a limit gets a close frame with status 1009.

`HTTP.WebSockets.open` with a URL accepts the client timeouts
`connect_timeout`, `request_timeout`, `response_header_timeout`,
`read_idle_timeout`, and `write_idle_timeout`. `read_idle_timeout` keeps
applying after the handshake: if nothing arrives for that long, the connection
closes and `receive` throws a `WebSocketError`.

### Compression

Pass `compress = true` to use the permessage-deflate extension
([RFC 7692](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7692)), which compresses each
message. Both sides must ask for it; otherwise messages are sent uncompressed.
`HTTP.WebSockets.listen!`, `HTTP.WebSockets.upgrade`, and
`HTTP.WebSockets.open` accept the keyword:

```julia
server = HTTP.WebSockets.listen!("127.0.0.1", 0; compress = true) do ws
    for msg in ws
        HTTP.WebSockets.send(ws, msg)
    end
end

HTTP.WebSockets.open("ws://" * HTTP.WebSockets.server_addr(server); compress = true) do ws
    HTTP.WebSockets.send(ws, repeat("compress me ", 1000))
    HTTP.WebSockets.receive(ws)
end
```

Compression helps most with large, repetitive text such as JSON. The
`maxframesize` limit applies to the decompressed message.

## HTTP/2

The client asks for HTTP/2 when it connects to an `https://` URL, and uses it
when the server agrees. Pass `prefer_http2 = false` to `HTTP.Client`, or
`protocol = :h1` to a single request, to use HTTP/1.1 instead.
`protocol = :h2` with an `http://` URL sends cleartext HTTP/2 without first
asking the server, which works with servers that accept it, including HTTP.jl's.

```julia
h1_only = HTTP.Client(prefer_http2 = false)
resp = HTTP.get(h1_only, "https://example.com")
close(h1_only)
```

Servers started with `HTTP.serve!` or `HTTP.listen!` speak HTTP/2 too. Over TLS,
the client and server agree on HTTP/2 during the TLS handshake, which is what
browsers require. On a plain listener, a client that opens with the HTTP/2
connection preface gets HTTP/2; pass `allow_h2c = false` to turn that off.
Requests with an `Upgrade: h2c` header are answered with HTTP/1.1.

### Flow-control windows

HTTP/2 flow control limits how many bytes can be in flight on a stream before
the receiver acknowledges them. With the protocol default window of 65,535
bytes, one stream can move at most about `window / round-trip time` per second,
which slows large transfers on high-latency links. Pass an
`HTTP.HTTP2Settings` as `http2_settings` to raise the receive windows.
The server's setting affects uploads and the client's affects downloads:

```julia
settings = HTTP.HTTP2Settings(
    initial_window_size = 1 << 20,     # 1 MiB per stream
    connection_window_size = 1 << 21,  # 2 MiB per connection
)

client = HTTP.Client(http2_settings = settings)
server = HTTP.serve!("127.0.0.1", 8080; http2_settings = settings) do req
    return HTTP.Response(200; body = "ok")
end
```

Both windows default to 65,535 bytes.

---

<!-- Page: https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/guides/migration-1x/ -->

# Migration From HTTP.jl 1.x

HTTP.jl 2.0 is a breaking release with a new HTTP stack underneath. Code that
calls `HTTP.get`, `HTTP.post`, `HTTP.request`, `HTTP.serve!`, `HTTP.Router`, and
`HTTP.WebSockets` usually needs only small changes. Code that used parser,
connection-pool, layer-stack, or other internal APIs has to move to the public
API. HTTP.jl 2.0 requires Julia 1.10 or later.

The snippets below assume `using HTTP` and an existing `url`.

## Checklist

- Read data written with `response_stream = io` from `io`; `resp.body` is
  `nothing`.
- Replace `HTTP.download` with `Downloads.download` or a `response_stream`
  file.
- Read text from a server request with `String(req.body)`.
- Use `HTTP.get_request_context(req)` for cancellation and deadlines.
- Replace `pool` with a long-lived `HTTP.Client`.
- Replace `retry_delays` and `retry_check` with `retries`, `retry_if`, and
  `HTTP.RetryBucket`.
- Replace `readtimeout` with the timeout keyword you need.
- Replace `sslconfig` with a `Transport`'s `tls_config`.
- Replace `HTTP.Exceptions.StatusError` and friends with the top-level names,
  and `HTTP.RequestError` with the underlying exception.
- Replace `Sockets.getpeername(stream)` with `HTTP.peeraddr(stream)`.
- Start servers with an interactive thread, such as `julia --threads=4,1`.
- Re-test redirects, retries, proxies, cookies, streaming, WebSockets,
  server-sent events, and HTTP/2.

## Response Bodies

`HTTP.request` and the verb helpers still return the whole body as a
`Vector{UInt8}` in `resp.body`. With `response_stream = io`, 1.x also stored
`io` in `resp.body`. In 2.0 `resp.body` is `nothing`; read the data from the
`io` you passed:

```julia
open("payload.bin", "w") do io
    resp = HTTP.get(url; response_stream = io)
    @assert resp.body === nothing
end
```

## `HTTP.download`

HTTP.jl 2.0 has no `download` function. `HTTP.download(url, path)` still runs,
because every module can see `Base.download`, but it calls `Base.download`,
which uses the Downloads standard library. It accepts none of HTTP.jl's
keywords; passing one throws a `MethodError`.

Use `Downloads.download` to copy a URL to a file:

```julia
using Downloads

Downloads.download(url, "payload.bin")
```

Stream the response into a file when you need HTTP.jl options such as headers,
retries, proxies, or a `Client`:

```julia
open("payload.bin", "w") do io
    HTTP.get(url; response_stream = io)
end
```

## Requests, Responses, and Headers

The 1.x positional constructors still work:

```julia
req = HTTP.Request("POST", "/widgets", ["Content-Type" => "text/plain"], "hello")
resp = HTTP.Response(201, ["Location" => "/widgets/1"], "created")
```

The keyword forms take the same values plus trailers, protocol version, and a
context:

```julia
req = HTTP.Request("POST", "/widgets"; headers = ["Content-Type" => "text/plain"], body = "hello")
```

`req.headers` and `resp.headers` are `HTTP.Headers`, an ordered vector of
`String => String` pairs; in 1.x they were a `Vector` of `SubString` pairs.
Header names keep the spelling you give them, and lookups such as
`HTTP.header(resp, "content-type")` ignore case. Headers received from the
network use `Content-Type` spelling, while 1.x kept the spelling from the wire.
Pass `canonicalize_headers = true` to send every request header name in that
form, as in 1.x. HTTP/2, which 2.0 uses for HTTPS when the server supports it,
always sends names in lowercase; pass `protocol = :h1` to a server that needs
exact spelling. Places that take headers still accept vectors of pairs.

## Request Context

`req.context` is still a `Dict{Symbol,Any}` for application data:

```julia
req.context[:request_id] = request_id
request_id = get(req.context, :request_id, nothing)
```

Cancellation and deadlines live on the `HTTP.RequestContext` returned by
`HTTP.get_request_context(req)`:

```julia
ctx = HTTP.get_request_context(req)
HTTP.set_deadline!(ctx, time_ns() + 5_000_000_000)
HTTP.canceled(ctx) && throw(HTTP.CanceledError("request canceled"))
```

## Clients, Proxies, and TLS

The `pool` keyword is ignored. Create a long-lived `HTTP.Client`
instead; it keeps connections, cookies, and settings across requests:

```julia
client = HTTP.Client(transport = HTTP.Transport(max_idle_per_host = 4))
try
    resp = HTTP.get(url; client = client)
finally
    close(client)
end
```

As in 1.x, requests without a `client` use proxies from the `HTTP_PROXY`,
`HTTPS_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY`, and `NO_PROXY` environment variables. 2.0 reads them
once, when the first such request runs, instead of on every request. The
`proxy` keyword accepts a proxy URL or an `HTTP.ProxyConfig`, and
`socks5://` and `socks5h://` proxies are supported:

```julia
HTTP.get(url; proxy = HTTP.ProxyURL("http://proxy.internal:8080"; no_proxy = "localhost"))
HTTP.get(url; proxy = HTTP.ProxyURL("socks5h://proxy.internal:1080"))
HTTP.get(url; proxy = nothing)  # connect directly
```

The `sslconfig` and `socket_type_tls` keywords are ignored. Configure TLS with a
`Reseau.TLS.Config` on the `Transport`:

```julia
using Reseau

client = HTTP.Client(transport = HTTP.Transport(tls_config = Reseau.TLS.Config(ca_file = "ca.pem")))
```

`require_ssl_verification = false` still turns off certificate checks for one
call.

## Retries

The `retry_delays` and `retry_check` keywords are ignored. A `retry_if`
function replaces `retry_check`. Return `true` to retry and `nothing` to fall
back to the default rules:

Before:

```julia
resp = HTTP.get(url; retries = 3, retry_delays = [0.1, 0.5, 1.0],
    retry_check = (s, ex, req, resp, resp_body) -> resp !== nothing && resp.status == 409)
```

After:

```julia
resp = HTTP.get(url; retries = 3, retry_if = (attempt, err, req, resp) ->
    resp !== nothing && resp.status == 409 ? true : nothing)
```

There is no list of delays. Retries wait a random, exponentially growing delay;
pass `retry_bucket = HTTP.RetryBucket(backoff_scale_factor_ms = 100)` to change
its scale. 2.0 retries 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, and 504 responses by default,
where 1.x also retried 403, 409, and every other 5xx status. See
[Retries](https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/guides/client/#Retries) in the client guide for the full default policy.

## Timeouts

`readtimeout` still works but is deprecated. It sets `read_idle_timeout`, the
longest wait between reads. Pick the timeout you mean:

```julia
resp = HTTP.get(url; connect_timeout = 5, request_timeout = 60, read_idle_timeout = 30)
```

[Timeouts](https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/guides/client/#Timeouts) in the client guide describes each keyword.
A timeout throws `HTTP.TimeoutError`, also available as `HTTP.HTTPTimeoutError`.

## Exceptions

The exception types live at the top level: `HTTP.StatusError`,
`HTTP.ConnectError`, `HTTP.TimeoutError`, and their supertype `HTTP.HTTPError`.
The 1.x names `HTTP.Exceptions.StatusError`, `ConnectError`, `TimeoutError`, and
`HTTPError` still resolve to them, with a deprecation warning under
`--depwarn=yes`. `@try` and `current_exceptions_to_string` are gone.

`HTTP.RequestError` is gone. Failures throw the underlying exception instead,
and `HTTP.isrecoverable` tells you whether a failure is worth retrying:

```julia
try
    HTTP.get(url)
catch e
    HTTP.isrecoverable(e) || rethrow()
    # a transient network failure; retry later
end
```

## `HTTP.@client`

`HTTP.@client` accepts one middleware or a tuple of them in each position. The
first middleware in a tuple is the outermost:

```julia
HTTP.@client request_middleware
HTTP.@client request_middleware stream_middleware
HTTP.@client (outer_request, inner_request) (outer_stream, inner_stream)
```

Request middleware wraps `request` and the verb helpers. Stream middleware wraps
`open`.

## Servers

`HTTP.serve!`, `HTTP.serve`, `HTTP.listen!`, `HTTP.listen`, and `HTTP.Router`
keep their 1.x shapes. Some details changed:

- Server tasks run on Julia's `:interactive` thread pool. Start Julia with at
  least one interactive thread; see the [server guide](https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/guides/server/).
- In a `serve!` handler, `req.body` is a body object rather than a
  `Vector{UInt8}`. Use `String(req.body)` to read it as text.
- `HTTP.peeraddr(stream)` replaces `Sockets.getpeername(stream)`. It returns
  the client address, or `nothing`; `string(addr)` gives `"ip:port"`.
- The server `readtimeout` keyword still works and sets `read_timeout`. Each
  server timeout has a seconds keyword (`read_timeout`) and a nanoseconds
  keyword (`read_timeout_ns`).

Before:

```julia
HTTP.listen("127.0.0.1", 8080) do stream
    ip, port = Sockets.getpeername(stream)
end
```

After:

```julia
HTTP.listen("127.0.0.1", 8080) do stream
    addr = HTTP.peeraddr(stream)
end
```

## WebSockets

The `HTTP.WebSockets` API keeps its 1.x shape: `open`, `listen!`, `listen`,
`upgrade`, `isupgrade`, `send`, `receive`, and iteration over a socket. Two
differences:

- `maxframesize` defaults to 16 MiB instead of no limit. Pass a larger value if
  your messages are bigger.
- `HTTP.WebSockets.upgrade` works only on HTTP/1.1 connections.

## Server-Sent Events

Clients still use the `sse_callback` keyword:

```julia
events = HTTP.SSEEvent[]
HTTP.request("GET", url; sse_callback = event -> push!(events, event))
```

Servers return the response that `HTTP.sse_stream` builds and write events in
its `do` block:

```julia
HTTP.serve!("127.0.0.1", 8080) do req
    return HTTP.sse_stream(200) do stream
        write(stream, HTTP.SSEEvent("ready"; event = "status", id = "1"))
    end
end
```

## Ignored 1.x Keywords

The client accepts these 1.x keywords so old calls do not fail, but they have no
effect and log a warning: `pool`, `retry_delays`, `retry_check`, `sslconfig`,
`socket_type_tls`, `detect_content_type`, `observelayers`, `logerrors`, and
`logtag`. `readtimeout` sets `read_idle_timeout`, and `canonicalize_headers`
keeps its 1.x meaning.

## Internal APIs

The 1.x layer stack, connection pool, parser, and socket/TLS extension points
have no 2.0 equivalent. Move that code to `Client`, `Transport`, `Stream`, the
server functions, `Router`, `HTTP.WebSockets`, or the SSE functions. If a use
case cannot be expressed with the public API, open an issue that describes it
instead of depending on 2.0 internals.

---

<!-- Page: https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/api/reference/ -->

# API Reference

These pages hold the docstrings of HTTP.jl's public API. The guides explain how
the pieces fit together.

## Module

### `HTTP` — Module

    HTTP

An HTTP client and server library for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, with WebSockets and
server-sent events. Reseau provides the TCP, DNS, and TLS layers.

- `request`, and `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`, `head`, `options`,
  and `query`, send a request and return the response.
- `open` streams a request and its response.
- `serve!` and `serve` run a server whose handler maps a `Request` to a
  `Response`.
- `listen!` and `listen` run a server whose handler reads and writes a
  `Stream`.
- `WebSockets` has the WebSocket client and server.
- `SSEEvent` and `sse_stream` send server-sent events.

## Reference Map

- [Core API](https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/api/core/): requests, responses, headers, errors, bodies, cookies, forms, proxies, and HTTP/2 settings.
- [Client API](https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/api/client/): `Client`, `Transport`, the request functions, streaming, retries, and trace events.
- [Server API](https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/api/server/): `Server`, `Stream`, routing, middleware, static files, and server-sent events.
- [WebSockets API](https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/api/websockets/): WebSocket clients, servers, and messages.

---

<!-- Page: https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/api/core/ -->

# Core API

## Core Messages and Errors

### `HTTP.Request` — Type

    Request(method, target; headers=Headers(), body=nothing, trailers=Headers(),
            host=nothing, content_length=-1, proto_major=1, proto_minor=1,
            close=false, context=RequestContext(), copyheaders=true)
    Request(method, target, headers[, body])

An HTTP request: what a server handler receives, and what the client sends.

- `headers`, `trailers`: anything `Headers` accepts. They are copied
  unless `copyheaders = false` and they are `Headers` collections; the request
  then uses them directly, so do not touch them while the request is in use.
- `body`: a `String`, a byte vector, an `AbstractBody`, or `nothing`.
- `host`: the authority sent as the HTTP/1 `Host` header or HTTP/2
  `:authority`.
- `content_length`: the body length in bytes. `-1` computes it for a
  `String`, byte-vector, or empty body, and means unknown for other bodies.
- `proto_major`, `proto_minor`: the HTTP version.
- `close`: close the connection after this request.
- `context`: the request's `RequestContext`.

`req.context` returns the context's application data as a `Dict{Symbol,Any}`;
use `get_request_context` for the `RequestContext` itself.

### `HTTP.Response` — Type

    Response(status, [body]; headers=Headers(), reason="", trailers=Headers(),
             content_length=-1, proto_major=1, proto_minor=1, close=false,
             request=nothing)
    Response(status, headers, body)
    Response(body)

An HTTP response: what a server handler returns, and what the client returns.

`body`, passed by position or as a keyword, may be a `String`, a byte vector,
an `AbstractBody`, or `nothing`. A `String` or byte vector is stored as
is, so one `Response` can be returned for many requests. `content_length`
defaults to the length of such a body. `request` is the request that produced
the response. `Response(body)` uses status 200.

A client response also has `response.url`, the final URL after redirects.

### `HTTP.Headers` — Type

    Headers()
    Headers(items)
    Headers(pairs...; kwargs...)

An ordered vector of `String => String` header pairs.

Header names match in any case (RFC 9110 §5.1): `header`, `setheader`,
`removeheader`, `haskey`, and the other lookups ignore case, and each name keeps
the spelling it was stored with. HTTP/1 sends names in that spelling; HTTP/2
sends them in lowercase. Headers read from the network are stored in
`canonical_header_key` form, such as `Content-Type`, so a response looks
the same over HTTP/1 and HTTP/2.

`items` may be a vector, dictionary, or tuple of pairs, and keyword arguments
add more headers. The input is copied, and a header with the same name as the
one before it is joined onto it, as in `appendheader`.
`Headers(n::Integer)` returns an empty collection with room for `n` headers.

### `HTTP.RequestContext` — Type

    RequestContext(; deadline_ns=0)

Cancellation, deadline, and application data for one request. Pass one to a
client call with the `context` keyword; `get_request_context` returns
the context of a request a server is handling.

`deadline_ns` is an absolute `time_ns()` value, or `0` for no deadline. A client
request still running at the deadline throws `TimeoutError`, and
`cancel!` makes it throw `CanceledError`.

Application data is stored under `Symbol` keys:

```julia
ctx = HTTP.RequestContext()
ctx[:request_id] = "abc"
get(ctx, :request_id, nothing)
```

### `HTTP.HTTPError` — Type

    HTTPError

Abstract supertype for HTTP-specific exceptions raised by HTTP.jl.

### `HTTP.ParseError` — Type

    ParseError

Raised when byte-level HTTP syntax cannot be parsed. This is used for malformed
request/status lines, invalid header syntax, truncated framed bodies, and other
wire-format failures where the peer did not send valid HTTP.

### `HTTP.ProtocolError` — Type

    ProtocolError

Raised when the bytes are syntactically valid but violate higher-level HTTP
rules. Examples include mismatched `Content-Length` values, impossible frame
ordering, or unsupported control-flow states in the client/server stacks.

### `HTTP.CanceledError` — Type

    CanceledError

Raised when request processing is canceled explicitly through `RequestContext`.
Unlike `ParseError` and `ProtocolError`, this usually reflects local control
flow rather than a bad peer.

### `HTTP.TimeoutError` — Type

    TimeoutError

Raised when a client timeout or deadline expires.

Fields:

- `operation::String`: `"connect"` or `"tls_handshake"` when `connect_timeout`
  expired, `"websocket handshake"` for a WebSocket handshake, and `"request"`
  for the other timeouts and for deadlines.
- `timeout_ns::Int64`: the timeout that expired, in nanoseconds, or `0` when it
  is not known.
- `elapsed_ns::Int64`: the time spent before it expired, in nanoseconds, or `0`
  when it is not known.

### `HTTP.HTTPTimeoutError` — Type

    HTTPTimeoutError

Another name for `TimeoutError`.

### `HTTP.StatusError` — Type

    StatusError

Raised by `request` and the verb helpers for a response with status 300 or
above that is not a redirect, unless `status_exception = false`.

Fields:

- `status::Int16`: the response status.
- `response::Response`: the response, including its body.

### `HTTP.TooManyRedirectsError` — Type

    TooManyRedirectsError

Raised when a request reaches its redirect limit and gets another redirect.
`limit` is the limit and `response` is the last redirect response.

### `HTTP.ConnectError` — Type

    ConnectError(address, cause)

Raised when the client cannot connect to `address` (`host:port`). `cause` is
the underlying exception.

### `HTTP.DNSError` — Type

    DNSError(hostname, cause)

Raised when the client cannot resolve `hostname`. `cause` is the underlying
exception.

### `HTTP.TLSHandshakeError` — Type

    TLSHandshakeError(cause)

Raised when a TLS handshake fails (other than a handshake timeout, which
surfaces as `TimeoutError` with `operation = "tls_handshake"`). TLS
failures after connection setup surface as `TLSTransportError` instead.

### `HTTP.TLSTransportError` — Type

    TLSTransportError(cause)

Raised when TLS-level I/O fails on an established connection during a request
— for example a connection reset or a truncated TLS stream while writing the
request or reading the response. `cause` is the underlying
`Reseau.TLS.TLSError`. TLS failures during connection setup surface as
`TLSHandshakeError` (or `TimeoutError` for handshake timeouts)
instead.

### `HTTP.AddressInUseError` — Type

    AddressInUseError(address)

Raised when a server cannot bind because the requested address is already in
use. `address` records the bind target (host:port).

## Header and Context Helpers

### `HTTP.canonical_header_key` — Function

    canonical_header_key(key) -> String

Return the header name `key` in canonical form, such as `Content-Type`: the
first letter and every letter after a `-` are uppercase, and the other ASCII
letters are lowercase. `key` is not checked for validity.

### `HTTP.header` — Function

    header(headers, key, default="")
    header(message, key, default="")

Return the first value of header `key`, or `default` if there is none. `key`
matches in any case. `message` is a `Request` or `Response`.

### `HTTP.headers` — Function

    headers(headers, key) -> Vector{String}
    headers(message, key) -> Vector{String}

Return every value of header `key`, in order, or `String[]` if there is none.

### `HTTP.hasheader` — Function

    hasheader(headers, key) -> Bool
    hasheader(message, key) -> Bool

Return `true` when header `key` is present and its first value is not empty.

    hasheader(headers, key, value) -> Bool

Return `true` when any stored header value for `key` matches `value`
case-insensitively.

### `HTTP.headercontains` — Function

    headercontains(headers, key, token) -> Bool
    headercontains(message, key, token) -> Bool

Return `true` when a value of header `key`, read as a comma-separated list,
contains `token`. Both the name and the token match in any case. Use it for
list-valued headers such as `Connection` and `Transfer-Encoding`.

### `HTTP.setheader` — Function

    setheader(headers, key => value) -> headers
    setheader(headers, key, value) -> headers
    setheader(message, key => value) -> message

Replace every value of header `key` with `value`. The header keeps the position
of its first occurrence and takes the spelling of `key`; a new header goes at
the end. `setheader!` is the same function.

    setheader(stream, key, value) -> nothing
    setheader(stream, key => value) -> nothing

Set a header of the response on a server `stream`. Call it before the first
write; after that it throws `ArgumentError`.

### `HTTP.setheader!` — Function

    setheader!(headers, key => value) -> headers
    setheader!(headers, key, value) -> headers
    setheader!(message, key => value) -> message

The same function as `setheader`.

### `HTTP.defaultheader!` — Function

    defaultheader!(headers, key => value) -> headers
    defaultheader!(message, key => value) -> message

Add `key => value` unless header `key` is already present.

### `HTTP.appendheader` — Function

    appendheader(headers, key => value) -> headers
    appendheader(headers, key, value) -> headers
    appendheader(message, key => value) -> message

Add a header value. When the last header has the same name, in any case, the
value is joined onto it instead: with `"; "` for `Cookie` (RFC 6265 §5.4) and
with `","` for other names (RFC 9110 §5.3). `Set-Cookie` values always become
separate headers. `appendheader!` is the same function.

### `HTTP.appendheader!` — Function

    appendheader!(headers, key => value) -> headers
    appendheader!(headers, key, value) -> headers
    appendheader!(message, key => value) -> message

The same function as `appendheader`.

### `HTTP.removeheader` — Function

    removeheader(headers, key) -> headers
    removeheader(message, key) -> message

Remove every value of header `key`. `removeheader!` is the same
function.

### `HTTP.removeheader!` — Function

    removeheader!(headers, key) -> headers
    removeheader!(message, key) -> message

The same function as `removeheader`.

### `HTTP.mkheaders` — Function

    mkheaders(headers_input) -> Headers

Convert `headers_input` to `Headers`. It may be `nothing`, a pair or 2-tuple, a
dictionary, or an iterable of pairs or 2-tuples. A `Headers` is returned as is,
without a copy. Each value, including each element of a vector value, is added
with `appendheader`, which joins it onto the previous header when the
names match.

### `HTTP.get_request_context` — Function

    get_request_context(request) -> RequestContext

Return the `RequestContext` of `request`, which holds its cancellation
state and deadline. `request.context` returns only the context's application
data.

### `HTTP.set_deadline!` — Function

    set_deadline!(ctx, deadline_ns) -> ctx

Set the deadline of `ctx` to `deadline_ns`, an absolute `time_ns()` value. `0`
removes the deadline.

### `HTTP.cancel!` — Function

    cancel!(ctx; message="request canceled") -> ctx

Cancel the request that uses `ctx`. Its current read or write stops, and the
request throws a `CanceledError` carrying `message`. `cancel!` does not
throw itself.

### `HTTP.canceled` — Function

    canceled(ctx) -> Bool

Return `true` once `cancel!` has been called on `ctx`.

### `HTTP.expired` — Function

    expired(ctx, now_ns=time_ns()) -> Bool

Return `true` when `ctx` has a deadline and `now_ns` has reached it.

## Body Types and Streamed Payloads

### `HTTP.AbstractBody` — Type

    AbstractBody

Supertype of request and response bodies that are read as a stream.

A subtype implements `body_read!`, `body_close!`, and
`body_closed`.

### `HTTP.CallbackBody` — Type

    CallbackBody(read_cb, close_cb)

A body produced by a function. `read_cb(dst::Vector{UInt8})` fills the start of
`dst` and returns the number of bytes written, or `0` at the end of the body.
`close_cb()` runs once, when the body is closed. A `CallbackBody` can be read
only once.

### `HTTP.nobody` — Constant

An empty `Vector{UInt8}` to pass as a body that has no bytes. It is shared, so do not modify it.

### `HTTP.body_read!` — Function

    body_read!(body, dst) -> Int

Read up to `length(dst)` bytes of `body` into `dst` and return how many were
read, or `0` at the end of the body.

### `HTTP.body_close!` — Function

    body_close!(body)

Close `body` and release what it holds. Closing a closed body does nothing, so
it is safe to call in a `finally` block.

### `HTTP.body_closed` — Function

    body_closed(body) -> Bool

Return `true` once `body_close!` has closed `body`. Reading a body to
the end does not close it.

### `HTTP.read_request` — Function

    read_request(io; max_line_bytes=64*1024, max_header_bytes=1024*1024) -> Request

Read one HTTP/1 request head from `io` and return it as a `Request` whose body
reads the rest of the request from `io`. `max_line_bytes` limits each line and
`max_header_bytes` the whole head. Throws `ParseError` or
`ProtocolError` for an invalid request.

### `HTTP.write_request!` — Function

    write_request!(io, request)

Write `request` to `io` in HTTP/1.1 format, with its body.

The `Host` header comes first (RFC 9110 §7.2), taken from the request's `Host`
header or else from `request.host`. A body of known length is sent with
`Content-Length`, and any other body with chunked encoding, the only framing
that carries trailers.

### `HTTP.write_response!` — Function

    write_response!(io, response, request=response.request)

Write `response` to `io` in HTTP/1.1 format, with its body. No body is written
for `1xx`, `204`, and `304` responses, or when `request` is a `HEAD` request.

### `HTTP.trailers` — Function

    trailers(body)

Return a copy of the trailers that ended a chunked `body`, or empty `Headers`
for other bodies. Read the body to the end first.

## Cookies, Forms, and Request Bodies

### `HTTP.Cookie` — Type

    Cookie(name, value; kwargs...)

A cookie, as sent in a request's `Cookie` header or a response's `Set-Cookie`
header. Set its other fields, such as `path`, `domain`, `expires`, `maxage`,
`secure`, `httponly`, and `samesite` (`:lax`, `:strict`, or `:none`), with
keywords.

### `HTTP.CookieJar` — Type

    CookieJar()
    CookieJar(entries::Dict{String, Dict{String, Cookie}})

An in-memory cookie store for a `Client` or the `cookiejar` keyword of
a request. It stores cookies from responses and picks the ones to send by their
domain, path, expiry, and `Secure` flag.

`jar.entries` holds the cookies, keyed by host. To keep cookies across
sessions, save `jar.entries` and later pass it to `CookieJar(entries)`, which
uses the `Dict` without copying it.

### `HTTP.cookies` — Function

    cookies(request_or_response) -> Vector{Cookie}

Return the cookies in a request's `Cookie` header or a response's `Set-Cookie`
headers.

### `HTTP.stringify` — Function

    stringify(cookie, isrequest=true) -> String
    stringify(prefix, cookies, isrequest=true) -> String

Format cookies as header text. With `isrequest = true` the result is
`name=value`, as in a `Cookie` header; with `false` it also has the attributes
of a `Set-Cookie` header, such as `Path`, `Domain`, and `HttpOnly`. The second
form appends `cookies` to the header text `prefix`, separated by `"; "`.

### `HTTP.getcookies!` — Function

    getcookies!(jar, scheme, host, path[, now]) -> Vector{Cookie}

Return the cookies from `jar` to send with a request to `scheme://host/path`.

### `HTTP.setcookies!` — Function

    setcookies!(jar, scheme, host, path, headers) -> nothing

Store the `Set-Cookie` headers of a response from `scheme://host/path` in `jar`.

### `HTTP.addcookie!` — Function

    addcookie!(message, cookie) -> message

Add `cookie` to the `Cookie` header of a `Request`, or as a new `Set-Cookie`
header of a `Response`.

### `HTTP.Form` — Type

    Form(parts; boundary, type=:formdata) <: IO

A multipart request body. `parts` is a collection of `name => value` pairs. An
`IO` value is streamed (an open file is sent with its file name, and a
`Multipart` with its own name and content type); any other value is
sent as `string(value)`. `type = :mixed` builds a `multipart/mixed` body
instead of `multipart/form-data`. A request with a `Form` body gets the
matching `Content-Type` header from `content_type`.

    Form(parts::Vector{<:Multipart}; boundary)

Build a `multipart/mixed` body from `parts`.

### `HTTP.Multipart` — Type

    Multipart(filename, data, contenttype="", contenttransferencoding="", name="") <: IO

One part of a multipart body, with its content in the `IO` `data`. `filename`
may be `nothing`, and an empty `contenttype` is detected from the data when the
part is sent. The `parse_multipart` functions return `Multipart`s, and
`Form` accepts them as values.

### `HTTP.Batch` — Function

    Batch(parts; boundary) -> Form

Build a `multipart/mixed` body, the format of batch APIs such as OData
`$batch`. `parts` is a vector of `Multipart`s or a collection of
`name => value` pairs, as for `Form` with `type = :mixed`.

```julia
parts = [
    HTTP.Multipart(nothing, IOBuffer("GET /users/1 HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n"), "application/http"),
    HTTP.Multipart(nothing, IOBuffer("GET /users/2 HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n"), "application/http"),
]
response = HTTP.post(url, [], HTTP.Batch(parts))
```

### `HTTP.content_type` — Function

    content_type(form) -> String

Return the `Content-Type` header value for `form`: `multipart/form-data` or
`multipart/mixed`, with the boundary.

### `HTTP.parse_multipart_form` — Function

    parse_multipart_form(content_type_header, body) -> Union{Vector{Multipart}, Nothing}
    parse_multipart_form(message) -> Union{Vector{Multipart}, Nothing}

Parse a `multipart/form-data` body, using the boundary in
`content_type_header`. The `message` form reads the `Content-Type` header and
body of a `Request` or `Response`, such as the request in a `serve!` handler.

Returns `nothing` when the content type is not `multipart/form-data` or there
is no body. Each `Multipart` has the part's `name`, `filename` (or
`nothing`), `contenttype`, and its content as the `IO` `data`.

#### Examples
```jldoctest
julia> body = Vector{UInt8}(
           "--boundary\r\n" *
           "Content-Disposition: form-data; name=\"greeting\"\r\n\r\n" *
           "hello\r\n" *
           "--boundary\r\n" *
           "Content-Disposition: form-data; name=\"file\"; filename=\"a.txt\"\r\n" *
           "Content-Type: text/plain\r\n\r\n" *
           "file contents\r\n" *
           "--boundary--\r\n");

julia> parts = HTTP.parse_multipart_form("multipart/form-data; boundary=boundary", body);

julia> length(parts)
2

julia> parts[1].name, String(read(parts[1].data))
("greeting", "hello")

julia> parts[2].name, parts[2].filename, parts[2].contenttype
("file", "a.txt", "text/plain")

julia> String(read(parts[2].data))
"file contents"
```

Inside a server handler, pass the request directly:

```julia
HTTP.serve!("127.0.0.1", 8080) do request
    parts = HTTP.parse_multipart_form(request)
    parts === nothing && return HTTP.Response(415, "expected multipart/form-data")
    return HTTP.Response(200, "received $(length(parts)) part(s)")
end
```

### `HTTP.parse_multipart` — Function

    parse_multipart(content_type_header, body, required_type=nothing) -> Union{Vector{Multipart}, Nothing}
    parse_multipart(message, required_type=nothing) -> Union{Vector{Multipart}, Nothing}

Parse a multipart body of any subtype, such as `multipart/form-data` or
`multipart/mixed`, using the boundary in `content_type_header`. The `message`
form reads the header and body of a `Request` or `Response`.

`required_type` (`:formdata` or `:mixed`) accepts only that subtype. Returns
`nothing` when the content type does not match or there is no body.

### `HTTP.parse_multipart_mixed` — Function

    parse_multipart_mixed(content_type_header, body) -> Union{Vector{Multipart}, Nothing}
    parse_multipart_mixed(message) -> Union{Vector{Multipart}, Nothing}

Parse a `multipart/mixed` body; see `parse_multipart`.

## Proxy Configuration

### `HTTP.ProxyConfig` — Type

    ProxyConfig(url; no_proxy=nothing)
    ProxyConfig(; http=nothing, https=nothing, all=nothing, no_proxy=nothing, env=false)

The proxy settings of a `Transport` or a request. `ProxyConfig()`
connects directly.

`http` is the proxy for `http://` URLs, `https` the proxy for `https://` URLs,
and `all` the proxy for either when the other is not set; `ProxyConfig(url)`
sets `all`. `no_proxy` is a `NoProxy`, or anything it accepts, naming
hosts to reach directly. With `env = true`, settings that are not given come
from the `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY`, and `NO_PROXY` environment
variables, in upper or lower case.

Proxy URLs may use `http://`, `socks5://`, or `socks5h://`; with either SOCKS
scheme, the proxy resolves host names. An `https://` proxy URL is accepted, but
a request through it throws `ArgumentError`.

### `HTTP.ProxyURL` — Function

    ProxyURL(url; no_proxy=nothing) -> ProxyConfig

Return a `ProxyConfig` that sends every request through the proxy at
`url`, except requests to the hosts in `no_proxy`.

### `HTTP.ProxyFromEnvironment` — Function

    ProxyFromEnvironment() -> ProxyConfig

Return a `ProxyConfig` read from the `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`,
`ALL_PROXY`, and `NO_PROXY` environment variables, in upper or lower case. The
variables are read once, when it is called. Requests to `localhost` and
loopback addresses never use these proxies.

### `HTTP.NoProxy` — Type

    NoProxy(spec)
    NoProxy()

The hosts that a `ProxyConfig` reaches without its proxy, in the format
of the `NO_PROXY` environment variable. `spec` is a comma-separated string or a
vector of entries: host names, domain suffixes, IP addresses, CIDR ranges, or
any of these with a `:port`. `"*"` matches every host. `localhost` and loopback
addresses always match.

## HTTP/2 Configuration

### `HTTP.HTTP2Settings` — Type

    HTTP2Settings(; initial_window_size=65535, connection_window_size=65535)

HTTP/2 receive windows, passed as `http2_settings` to a `Client` or to
`serve!` and `listen!`.

- `initial_window_size`: the receive window of each stream, sent as
  `SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE` (RFC 9113 §6.5.2). Values from 1 to 2^31 - 1
  are allowed, so it can also be lowered to slow down senders.
- `connection_window_size`: the receive window shared by all streams on a
  connection, from 65535 to 2^31 - 1.

Both default to 65535, the protocol default. One stream can move at most about
`window / round-trip time` bytes per second, so raise them for large transfers
over links with high latency.

---

<!-- Page: https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/api/client/ -->

# Client API

## Client Types and Operations

### `HTTP.Transport` — Type

    Transport(; tls_config=nothing, proxy=nothing, retry_bucket=RetryBucket(),
              max_idle_per_host=2, max_idle_total=64, max_conns_per_host=0,
              idle_timeout_ns=90_000_000_000, max_header_bytes=1024*1024,
              max_line_bytes=64*1024, local_addr=nothing)

The connection pool of a `Client`, with the settings for opening
connections.

- `tls_config`: a `Reseau.TLS.Config` for `https://` connections.
- `proxy`: a `ProxyConfig`, a proxy URL, or `nothing` to connect
  directly. A `Client` created without a `transport` uses
  `ProxyFromEnvironment` instead.
- `retry_bucket`: the `RetryBucket` that limits retries, or `nothing`.
- `max_idle_per_host`, `max_idle_total`: how many idle HTTP/1 connections to
  keep for one host and in all.
- `max_conns_per_host`: the most HTTP/1 connections to one host, counting idle,
  busy, and opening ones; further requests wait for one. `0` means no limit.
- `idle_timeout_ns`: how long, in nanoseconds, an idle HTTP/1 or HTTP/2
  connection stays reusable; `0` means no limit. Keep it below the idle timeout
  of NATs and load balancers on the path, often a few minutes, so that requests
  are not sent on connections they dropped. A response header
  `Keep-Alive: timeout=N` shortens it to `N - 1` seconds for that connection.
- `max_line_bytes`, `max_header_bytes`: the longest HTTP/1 response line and the
  largest response head (and chunked trailers); a longer one fails the request
  with a `ProtocolError`. `max_line_bytes` defaults to the smaller of
  64 KiB and `max_header_bytes`. Raise it for servers that send very long
  header lines, such as large `Content-Security-Policy` values.
- `local_addr`: the source IP address of connections, as a string or a
  `Reseau.TCP.SocketAddrV4`/`SocketAddrV6`.

### `HTTP.Client` — Type

    Client(; transport=Transport(proxy=ProxyFromEnvironment()), cookiejar=CookieJar(),
           max_redirects=10, check_redirect=nothing, prefer_http2=true,
           http2_settings=HTTP2Settings(), default_headers=[], default_query=nothing,
           default_basicauth=nothing, connect_timeout=0, request_timeout=0,
           response_header_timeout=0, read_idle_timeout=0, write_idle_timeout=0,
           local_addr=nothing)

An HTTP client: a connection pool plus the settings and cookies that requests
sent through it share. Pass it to `request`, the verb helpers, or `open` as the
first argument or as the `client` keyword. Calls without a client use a shared
default `Client`. `close(client)` closes its connections; using a closed client
throws `ArgumentError`.

- `transport`: the `Transport` that owns the connections. The default
  one takes its proxy from the environment.
- `cookiejar`: the `CookieJar` for this client, or `nothing` for no
  cookies.
- `max_redirects`: the most redirects one request follows.
- `check_redirect`: a function `(response, request, location) -> Bool`; return
  `false` to stop at a redirect and return it.
- `prefer_http2`: try HTTP/2 for `https://` URLs. When an origin turns out to
  speak only HTTP/1.1, the client remembers that until
  `close_idle_connections!`. `protocol = :h2` on a call always tries
  HTTP/2.
- `http2_settings`: the `HTTP2Settings` for HTTP/2 connections.
- `default_headers`: headers added to each request that does not set them.
- `default_query`: query parameters added to each URL; the call's `query`
  replaces those with the same key.
- `default_basicauth`: `user => password` used unless the call passes
  `basicauth` or an `Authorization` header.
- `connect_timeout`, `request_timeout`, `response_header_timeout`,
  `read_idle_timeout`, `write_idle_timeout`: timeouts in seconds, used when the
  call passes no value or `0`. `0` here means no default.
- `local_addr`: the source IP address for connections, as a string or a
  `Reseau.TCP.SocketAddrV4`/`SocketAddrV6`. With your own `transport`, set it on
  the `Transport` instead.

### `HTTP.RetryBucket` — Type

    RetryBucket(; backoff_scale_factor_ms=25, max_backoff_secs=20, capacity=500)

A retry budget shared by the requests of a `Transport`, so that a burst
of failures does not become a burst of retries. Each host has its own budget of
`capacity`. A retry reserves part of it; the reservation comes back when the
retried attempt gets a response that is not worth retrying, and is kept, in
whole or in part, when the attempt fails again. Each request that succeeds
without a retry earns back one unit. When a host's budget runs out, failures
are not retried, and a `RetrySkippedEvent` with reason `:retry_bucket`
reports it.

Retries wait a random time of up to `backoff_scale_factor_ms * 2^(attempt - 1)`
milliseconds, and at most `max_backoff_secs` seconds.

### `HTTP.RequestRetryError` — Type

    RequestRetryError(err)

What a `retry_if` function receives as `err` when an attempt failed without a
response. `err.err` is the exception.

### `HTTP.retry_attempts` — Function

    retry_attempts(request) -> Int
    retry_attempts(response) -> Int

Return how many times the client retried the request, `0` when the first
attempt was the only one. The count is also stored as
`request.context[:retryattempt]`.

### `HTTP.isrecoverable` — Function

    isrecoverable(err::Exception) -> Bool

Return `true` when `err` is a transient failure that the client's default retry
rules retry: a connection that was reset or closed early, a socket error, a
malformed response, a connect or TLS handshake timeout, or an HTTP/2 stream the
server refused. An expired deadline and other errors return `false`. `err` may
also be the `RequestRetryError` that a `retry_if` function receives.

### `HTTP.roundtrip!` — Function

    roundtrip!(transport, address, request; secure=false, server_name=nothing) -> Response

Send `request` to `address` (`"host:port"`) over one HTTP/1 connection from
`transport`, without redirects, cookies, or the client's retry rules.
`secure = true` uses TLS,
with `server_name` for SNI and certificate checks. The response body is a
stream; read it with `body_read!` and close it with
`body_close!`.

### `HTTP.request` — Function

    request(method, url, headers=[], body=nothing; kwargs...) -> Response
    request(trace, method, url, headers=[], body=nothing; kwargs...) -> Response

Send an HTTP request and return the `Response`, with the whole body in
`response.body` as a `Vector{UInt8}`.

`url` is a string or `URI`. `headers` is anything `Headers` accepts.
`body` may be a `String`, a byte vector, an `IO`, a `Dict` or `NamedTuple` (sent
as a URL-encoded form), a `Form`, an iterable of string or byte chunks,
or an `AbstractBody`. `headers` and `body` can also be passed as
keywords. Unless the request sets them, HTTP.jl sends
`User-Agent: HTTP.jl/<version>` and `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate`.

A response with status 300 or above throws a `StatusError`, except for
redirect responses (301, 302, 303, 307, and 308). A timeout throws a
`TimeoutError`, and a failure to connect throws an error such as
`ConnectError` or `DNSError`.

!!! warning "`String(response.body)` empties `response.body`"
    `String(::Vector{UInt8})` takes over the vector's memory instead of copying
    it, so `response.body` is empty afterwards. Use `String(copy(response.body))`
    if you need the bytes again.

#### Keywords

Request and response:
- `query`: a `Dict`, `NamedTuple`, vector of pairs, or string to add to the
  URL's query string.
- `basicauth`: credentials as `user => password` or `(user, password)`. An
  `Authorization` header takes precedence; credentials in the URL are used when
  neither is given.
- `status_exception = true`: throw `StatusError` for a failing response.
- `response_stream`: an `IO` or byte vector that receives the body instead of
  `response.body`, which is then `nothing` for an `IO` and the filled vector or
  view otherwise. A byte vector must be large enough for the body, and is
  resized to it if it is a `Vector{UInt8}`. A response with status 300 or
  above, including a redirect that is not followed, leaves a byte vector
  untouched and puts up to 1 MiB of its body (or `max_decompressed_size`, if
  smaller) in `response.body`.
- `decompress = true`: decompress gzip and deflate responses. `false` returns
  the body as sent and does not send `Accept-Encoding`.
- `max_decompressed_size = 64 MiB`: the largest decompressed body; a larger one
  throws `DecompressionLimitError`. `0` means no limit.
- `sse_callback`: for a server-sent event stream, call `f(event)` or
  `f(stream, event)` with each `SSEEvent` instead of reading the body.
  `max_sse_line_bytes = 1 MiB` and `max_sse_event_bytes = 16 MiB` limit the
  size of a line and an event; `0` means no limit.
- `copyheaders = true`: `false` lets the request use an `HTTP.Headers`
  collection without copying it. Do not touch it until the call returns; its
  contents afterwards are unspecified.
- `canonicalize_headers = false`: `true` sends header names in
  `canonical_header_key` form. Otherwise names are sent as given, and
  HTTP/2 sends them in lowercase.

Redirects:
- `redirect = true`: follow redirects.
- `redirect_limit`: the most redirects to follow; defaults to the client's
  `max_redirects`, 10 by default. With `0`, the redirect response is returned.
- `redirect_method`: the method for following a 301 or 302 redirect, or
  `:same` to keep the original method. By default `GET` is used, except that
  `HEAD` and `QUERY` are kept. A 303 always uses `GET`, and 307 and 308 keep the
  method.
- `forwardheaders = true`: send the request's headers again when following a
  redirect. Credentials are dropped when the redirect goes to another origin.

Retries (see the client guide for the default rules):
- `retry = true`: retry failed attempts. An idempotent request that fails on a
  reused connection the server already closed is resent either way.
- `retries = 4`: the most retries after the first attempt.
- `retry_non_idempotent = false`: also retry methods other than `GET`, `HEAD`,
  `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`, `QUERY`, `PUT`, and `DELETE`.
- `retry_if`: a function `(attempt, err, req, resp)` that returns `true` to
  retry, `false` to stop, or `nothing` for the default rules. For a failure
  without a response, `err` is a `RequestRetryError` and `resp` is
  `nothing`; for a response, `err` is `nothing`. A body that cannot be sent again
  is never retried.
- `respect_retry_after = true`: wait as long as a 429 or 503 response's
  `Retry-After` header asks.
- `retry_bucket = true`: use the transport's `RetryBucket` to limit
  retries; pass `false` to skip it, or another `RetryBucket`.

Timeouts, in seconds:
- `connect_timeout`: DNS lookup, TCP connect, proxy handshake, TLS handshake,
  and HTTP/2 setup. Defaults to the client's `connect_timeout`, or 30.
- `request_timeout`: the whole call.
- `response_header_timeout`: the wait for the response headers.
- `read_idle_timeout`: the time between reads, including the wait for the
  response headers.
- `write_idle_timeout`: the time between writes.
- `expect_continue_timeout`: how long a request with an
  `Expect: 100-continue` header waits for `100 Continue` before it sends the
  body anyway, 1 second by default. `0` sends the body without waiting.
- `context`: a `RequestContext` for cancellation and an absolute
  deadline.

Connections:
- `client`: the `Client` to use; defaults to a shared client.
- `proxy`: a proxy URL, a `ProxyConfig`, or `nothing` to connect
  directly. Cannot be combined with `client`; set the proxy on its `Transport`.
- `cookies = true`: send and store cookies with the cookie jar. `false` turns
  cookies off, and a `Dict` adds name/value pairs. Cookies from the jar are
  merged into a `Cookie` header set on the request.
- `cookiejar`: the `CookieJar` to use; defaults to the client's jar, or
  `HTTP.COOKIEJAR` for calls without a client.
- `require_ssl_verification = true`: `false` skips certificate checks, for
  testing only. Cannot be combined with `client`.
- `protocol = :auto`: `:h1` or `:h2` to force HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2.

Debugging:
- `verbose`: `1` (or `true`) prints a line for each attempt, response, retry,
  redirect, and the result; `2` also prints the request and response heads.
- `trace`: a function called with each `RequestEvent`,
  `ResponseHeadEvent`, `RetryEvent`,
  `RetrySkippedEvent`, `RedirectEvent`, and
  `DoneEvent`.

#### Extended help

These HTTP.jl 1.x keywords are accepted but have no effect, and log a warning:
`pool`, `retry_delays`, `retry_check`, `sslconfig`, `socket_type_tls`,
`detect_content_type`, `observelayers`, `logerrors`, and `logtag`. The
deprecated `readtimeout` sets `read_idle_timeout`.

### `HTTP.get` — Function

    get(headers, key, default)

Dict-style `get` on `Headers`. Returns the first value for `key`, including
an empty value, or `default` if the header is absent.

    get(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    head(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    options(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    post(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    put(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    patch(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    delete(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    query(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response

Send a request with the method in the function's name: `HTTP.get(url)` is
`HTTP.request("GET", url)`. Each takes the keywords of `request`,
including `headers` and `body`, and also accepts a `Client` as its first
argument.

### `HTTP.head` — Function

    get(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    head(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    options(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    post(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    put(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    patch(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    delete(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    query(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response

Send a request with the method in the function's name: `HTTP.get(url)` is
`HTTP.request("GET", url)`. Each takes the keywords of `request`,
including `headers` and `body`, and also accepts a `Client` as its first
argument.

### `HTTP.query` — Function

    get(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    head(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    options(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    post(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    put(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    patch(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    delete(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    query(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response

Send a request with the method in the function's name: `HTTP.get(url)` is
`HTTP.request("GET", url)`. Each takes the keywords of `request`,
including `headers` and `body`, and also accepts a `Client` as its first
argument.

### `HTTP.post` — Function

    get(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
