    head(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    options(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    post(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    put(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    patch(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    delete(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    query(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response

Send a request with the method in the function's name: `HTTP.get(url)` is
`HTTP.request("GET", url)`. Each takes the keywords of `request`,
including `headers` and `body`, and also accepts a `Client` as its first
argument.

### `HTTP.put` — Function

    get(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    head(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    options(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    post(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    put(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    patch(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    delete(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    query(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response

Send a request with the method in the function's name: `HTTP.get(url)` is
`HTTP.request("GET", url)`. Each takes the keywords of `request`,
including `headers` and `body`, and also accepts a `Client` as its first
argument.

### `HTTP.patch` — Function

    get(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    head(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    options(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    post(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    put(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    patch(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    delete(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    query(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response

Send a request with the method in the function's name: `HTTP.get(url)` is
`HTTP.request("GET", url)`. Each takes the keywords of `request`,
including `headers` and `body`, and also accepts a `Client` as its first
argument.

### `HTTP.delete` — Function

    get(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    head(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    options(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    post(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    put(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    patch(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    delete(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    query(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response

Send a request with the method in the function's name: `HTTP.get(url)` is
`HTTP.request("GET", url)`. Each takes the keywords of `request`,
including `headers` and `body`, and also accepts a `Client` as its first
argument.

### `HTTP.options` — Function

    get(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    head(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    options(url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Response
    post(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    put(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    patch(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    delete(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response
    query(url, [headers], [body]; kwargs...) -> Response

Send a request with the method in the function's name: `HTTP.get(url)` is
`HTTP.request("GET", url)`. Each takes the keywords of `request`,
including `headers` and `body`, and also accepts a `Client` as its first
argument.

### `HTTP.open` — Function

    open(method, url, headers=[]; kwargs...) -> Stream
    open(f, method, url, headers=[]; status_exception=true, kwargs...) -> Response

Send a request and stream its body and response through a `Stream`.
Write the request body to the stream, call `startread` to finish the
request and get the response status and headers, then read the response body
from the stream like any `IO`.

With a function `f`, `open` calls `f(stream)`, finishes the exchange, and
returns the final `Response`, not the value of `f`. It throws a
`StatusError` for a failing response unless `status_exception = false`.
Without `f`, close the stream with `closewrite` and `closeread` when you
are done.

`open` follows redirects, retries, decompresses, and applies timeouts like
`request`, and takes its keywords except `body`, `response_stream`,
`sse_callback`, `trace`, `verbose`, and the size limits.

```julia
buf = IOBuffer()
response = HTTP.open("GET", "https://example.com") do stream
    write(buf, stream)  # copy the body as it arrives
end
```

### `HTTP.do!` — Function

    do!(client, address, request; secure=false, server_name=nothing, protocol=:auto,
        redirect_limit=nothing, redirect_method=nothing, forwardheaders=true,
        cookies=true, cookiejar=nothing, context=nothing) -> Response

Send a prepared `request` to `address` (`"host:port"`) through `client`,
following redirects and using cookies like `request`, but without
retries or status errors. `secure = true` connects with TLS.

The response body is a stream: read it with `body_read!` and close it
with `body_close!`.

### `HTTP.get!` — Function

    get!(client, address, target; secure=false, protocol=:auto, kwargs...) -> Response

Send a `GET` request for `target` to `address` with `do!`.

### `HTTP.@client` — Macro

    HTTP.@client request_middleware
    HTTP.@client request_middleware stream_middleware

Define `request`, the verb helpers (`get`, `post`, ...), and `open` in the
calling module so that they pass through middleware before reaching HTTP.jl.

A middleware is a function `mw(next) -> f`. Request middleware returns
`f(method, url, headers, body; kwargs...)`, which handles `request` and the verb
helpers. Stream middleware returns `f(method, url, headers; kwargs...)`, which
handles `open`. Each position takes one middleware or a tuple of them; in
`(outer, inner)`, `outer` runs first.

### `HTTP.close_idle_connections!` — Function

    close_idle_connections!()
    close_idle_connections!(client::HTTP.Client)
    close_idle_connections!(transport::HTTP.Transport)

Close the idle connections in a pool; requests in progress are not affected.
Without an argument, it uses the shared client of calls that pass no `client`.

The `Client` and no-argument forms also close idle HTTP/2 connections, and
forget which origins answered with HTTP/1.1, so later requests try HTTP/2 with
them again. The `Transport` form covers only its HTTP/1 connections.

### `HTTP.idle_connection_count` — Function

    idle_connection_count(transport; key=nothing) -> Int

Return the number of idle HTTP/1 connections in `transport`, or only those for
`key`, a scheme and address such as `"https://example.com:443"`.

### `HTTP.isaborted` — Function

    isaborted(stream) -> Bool

Return `true` when the response on a client `stream` ended in an error, so its
connection cannot be reused.

## Request Trace Events

### `HTTP.RequestEvent` — Type

    RequestEvent

Trace event emitted immediately before a high-level request attempt is sent.

Fields:
- `request`: request head/body metadata for the attempt
- `url`: absolute request URL for the attempt
- `attempt`: 1-based request attempt number
- `redirect_count`: number of redirects already followed before this attempt
- `protocol`: `:h1` or `:h2` for the selected wire protocol

### `HTTP.ResponseHeadEvent` — Type

    ResponseHeadEvent

Trace event emitted after response headers are available for a successful
request attempt and before the body is fully consumed.

Fields:
- `response`: response head metadata for the attempt
- `url`: absolute request URL for the attempt
- `attempt`: 1-based request attempt number
- `redirect_count`: number of redirects followed before this response

### `HTTP.RetryEvent` — Type

    RetryEvent

Trace event emitted when the high-level request path schedules another attempt.

Fields:
- `request`: request metadata that will be retried
- `url`: absolute request URL for the attempt being retried
- `attempt`: current 1-based attempt number
- `next_attempt`: next 1-based attempt number
- `redirect_count`: redirects already followed when the retry decision was made
- `delay_ns`: delay before the next attempt in nanoseconds
- `response`: retry-triggering response, or `nothing` for request-path failures
- `err`: retry-triggering exception, or `nothing` for response-based retries

### `HTTP.RetrySkippedEvent` — Type

    RetrySkippedEvent

Trace event emitted when the retry policy wanted to retry an attempt but the
retry was not armed, so the attempt's failure becomes the request's outcome.
Without this event a denied retry is indistinguishable from a non-retryable
failure.

Fields:
- `request`: request metadata for the attempt that will not be retried
- `url`: absolute request URL for the attempt
- `attempt`: current 1-based attempt number
- `redirect_count`: redirects already followed when the retry decision was made
- `reason`: `:retry_bucket` when the transport's `RetryBucket` denied
  retry capacity; `:deadline` when the request deadline preempted the retry
  backoff
- `response`: retry-triggering response, or `nothing` for request-path failures
- `err`: retry-triggering exception, or `nothing` for response-based retries

### `HTTP.RedirectEvent` — Type

    RedirectEvent

Trace event emitted when a redirect response is accepted and a follow-up request
is about to be issued.

Fields:
- `request`: original request metadata that produced the redirect response
- `response`: redirect response head
- `from_url`: original absolute request URL
- `to_url`: resolved redirect target URL
- `redirect_count`: 1-based redirect count after accepting this redirect

### `HTTP.DoneEvent` — Type

    DoneEvent

Trace event emitted when a high-level request call finishes, either with a
final response or an exception.

Fields:
- `response`: final response, or `nothing` if the request failed before one was produced
- `err`: terminal exception, or `nothing` when the request completed successfully
- `url`: absolute request URL for the overall call

---

<!-- Page: https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/api/server/ -->

# Server API

## Server Lifecycle and Request Handlers

### `HTTP.Server` — Type

    Server(; network="tcp", address="127.0.0.1:0", handler, stream=false, ...)

An HTTP server, returned by `serve!` and `listen!`.
`port` returns its port. `close(server)` stops accepting connections and
waits for the requests in progress to finish, `forceclose` closes every
connection at once, and `wait(server)` returns when the server stops accepting
connections.

Server tasks, including handlers, run on Julia's `:interactive` thread pool.
Start Julia with at least one interactive thread, such as `--threads=4,1`, so
that tasks on the default pool that never yield cannot stall the server.
Without an interactive thread, these tasks run on the default pool.

On a plain TCP listener, a connection that starts with the HTTP/2 connection
preface is served as cleartext HTTP/2; `allow_h2c = false` turns that off. A
TLS listener offers HTTP/2 when its `TLS.Config` lists `"h2"` in
`alpn_protocols`.

The constructor takes the keywords of `serve!` with timeouts in nanoseconds
only; `stream = true` marks `handler` as a stream handler. Start the server with
`listen!(server)`.

### `HTTP.Stream` — Type

    Stream

One HTTP exchange, read and written as an `IO`. A server passes one to each
stream handler, and the client's `open` returns one.

On a server stream, `startread` returns the request, reading the stream
reads the request body, and `setstatus`, `setheader`, and
writes build the response. On a client stream, writes send the request body,
and after `startread` reading the stream reads the response body.

### `HTTP.listen!` — Function

    listen!(server) -> Server

Start `server`, made with the `Server` constructor, in the background
and return it.

    listen!(handler, host="127.0.0.1", port=8080; kwargs...) -> Server
    listen!(handler, port; kwargs...) -> Server
    listen!(handler, listener; kwargs...) -> Server

Start an HTTP server in the background and return its `Server`.
`handler(stream::Stream)` reads each request from the `Stream` and
writes the response to it. `listen!` takes the keywords of `serve!`
except `max_body_bytes`, since a stream handler reads the body itself.

### `HTTP.listen` — Function

    listen(handler, args...; kwargs...) -> Server

Like `listen!`, but block until the server is closed.

### `HTTP.serve!` — Function

    serve!(handler, host="127.0.0.1", port=8080; kwargs...) -> Server
    serve!(handler, port; kwargs...) -> Server
    serve!(handler, listener; kwargs...) -> Server

Start an HTTP server in the background and return its `Server`.
`handler(req::Request)` returns the `Response` for each request; a
handler that throws sends `500 Internal Server Error`. Port `0` picks a free
port. `listener` is a listener from `Reseau.TCP.listen` or
`Reseau.TLS.listen`; pass a TLS listener to serve HTTPS. Server tasks run on
Julia's `:interactive` thread pool; see `Server`.

#### Keywords

- `read_header_timeout`, `read_timeout`, `write_timeout`, `idle_timeout`:
  timeouts in seconds, all off by default. Each also has a nanosecond form
  ending in `_ns`, such as `read_timeout_ns`. `read_header_timeout` limits
  reading a request's head, `read_timeout` then limits reading its body, and
  `idle_timeout` limits the wait for the next request on a kept-alive
  connection. The header and idle timeouts fall back to `read_timeout` when
  they are `0`. A request whose head or body times out gets
  `408 Request Timeout`.
- `max_body_bytes = 64 MiB`: the largest request body `serve!` reads into
  memory; a larger one gets `413 Content Too Large`. `0` means no limit.
- `max_header_bytes = 1 MiB`: the largest request head.
- `http2_settings`: the `HTTP2Settings` for HTTP/2 connections.
- `max_concurrent_streams = 100`: the most HTTP/2 streams a connection may
  have open; `0` means no limit.
- `allow_h2c = true`: serve cleartext HTTP/2 to clients that send the HTTP/2
  connection preface.
- `listenany = false`: `true` ignores `port` and listens on a free port.
- `reuseaddr = true`, `backlog = 128`: options for the listener that `serve!`
  creates; they do not apply to a `listener` argument.

#### Extended help

`readtimeout` is a deprecated name for `read_timeout`.

### `HTTP.serve` — Function

    serve(handler, args...; kwargs...) -> Server

Like `serve!`, but block until the server is closed.

### `HTTP.streamhandler` — Function

    streamhandler(request_handler) -> stream handler

Return a stream handler, for `listen!`, that reads each request into memory,
calls `request_handler(req)`, and writes the response it returns. A response
body that is not in memory, such as a file from `fileserver`, is streamed.

### `HTTP.servefile` — Function

    servefile(request, path; index_file="index.html", redirect_canonical=true,
              etag=nothing, cache_control=nothing) -> Response

Build the response to `request` for the file or directory at `path`, with the
conditional and range handling of `servecontent`. A directory is served
by its `index_file`. With `redirect_canonical`, a request for a directory
without a trailing slash, a file with one, or the index file itself is
redirected to the canonical path. Methods other than `GET` and `HEAD` get
`405`, a missing file `404`, and an unsafe request path, such as one with
`..`, `400`.

`etag` may be `:weak_stat`, for an ETag made from the file's size and
modification time, a function `(path, stat) -> String`, or a string; by default
no ETag is sent. `cache_control` sets the `Cache-Control` header.

### `HTTP.fileserver` — Function

    fileserver(root; index_file="index.html", redirect_canonical=true, etag=nothing,
               cache_control=nothing, spa_fallback=nothing) -> handler

Return a request handler that serves the files under the directory `root` with
`servefile`, which describes the keywords. With `spa_fallback`, a
missing path whose last segment does not look like a file name, such as
`/users/42`, gets the file `spa_fallback` from `root`, as a single-page app
needs; a missing path such as `/app.js` still gets `404`. Throws
`ArgumentError` when `root` is not an existing directory.

### `HTTP.servecontent` — Function

    servecontent(request, source; name="", size=nothing, modtime=nothing,
                 content_type=nothing, etag=nothing, headers=Headers(),
                 allow_ranges=true) -> Response

Build the response to `request` for `source`, an `AbstractVector{UInt8}` or a
seekable `IO`; pass `codeunits(str)` for a string. Conditional requests
(`If-None-Match`, `If-Modified-Since`, `If-Match`, `If-Unmodified-Since`) get
`304` or `412` when they apply. A `GET` or `HEAD` request for one byte range
gets `206 Partial Content`, and an unsatisfiable range gets `416`. Any other
`Range`, such as several ranges or another unit, is ignored and the whole
content is sent.

- `name`: a file name whose extension sets the `Content-Type` when
  `content_type` is not given. Without either, the type is detected from the
  content.
- `size`: the length of `source`, needed when it cannot be found by seeking.
- `modtime`: a `DateTime` sent as `Last-Modified`.
- `etag`: the `ETag` value.
- `headers`: more response headers.
- `allow_ranges`: answer `Range` requests.

### `HTTP.forceclose` — Function

    forceclose(server)

Stop `server` at once: stop accepting connections and close every open
connection, including those with requests in progress.

### `HTTP.port` — Function

    port(server) -> Int

Return the port `server` listens on, or the configured port before it starts
listening.

### `HTTP.startread` — Function

    startread(stream)

Start reading from `stream` and return the message head.

On a client stream from `open`, this finishes sending the request and
returns the `Response` with its status and headers. On a server stream,
it returns the `Request`. Either way, read the body from `stream`
itself, with `read(stream)` or `readbytes!(stream, buf)`.

### `HTTP.startwrite` — Function

    startwrite(stream) -> Response

Start the response of a server-side `Stream` and return the response metadata.
`write(stream, data)` starts it too.

Chunked and HTTP/2 responses send their head here. A fixed-length
(`Content-Length`) HTTP/1 response holds its head and body so that a small
response goes out in one write. Without an explicit `startwrite`, the whole
body is held until `closewrite`, so the server can still send an error response
if the handler throws or writes the wrong number of bytes. After `startwrite`,
a body that grows past 4 KiB is sent as it is written, and a later failure
closes the connection instead.

### `HTTP.setstatus` — Function

    setstatus(stream, status) -> nothing

Set the status of the response on a server `stream`. Call it before the first
write; after that it throws `ArgumentError`.

### `HTTP.addtrailer` — Function

    addtrailer(stream, key => value) -> nothing
    addtrailer(stream, headers) -> nothing

Add trailers to the response on a server `stream`. They are sent after the body,
so add them before `closewrite(stream)`. Only chunked HTTP/1 and HTTP/2
responses carry trailers; an HTTP/1 response with a `Content-Length` drops them.

### `HTTP.closeread` — Function

    closeread(stream) -> Response

Stop reading from `stream` and return its `Response`: the response
received on a client stream, or the response being written on a server stream.
Body bytes that were not read are discarded, and the connection is then closed
instead of reused.

### `HTTP.peeraddr` — Function

    peeraddr(stream::Stream) -> Union{Nothing, Reseau.TCP.SocketAddr}

Return the client's address for a server `stream`, or `nothing` when it is not
known. `string(addr)` gives `"ip:port"`; `addr.ip` is a tuple of the address
bytes and `addr.port` is the port. Works over HTTP/1 and HTTP/2, with or without
TLS. Throws `ArgumentError` for a client stream.

## Routing and Middleware

The router and middleware live in `HTTP.Handlers`. Except for `handlertimeout`
and `logging_middleware`, the names below are also available from `HTTP`
directly, as in `HTTP.Router` and `HTTP.register!`.

### `HTTP.Handlers.Handler` — Type

    Handler

The name of the handler interface. Nothing subtypes or dispatches on it.

A handler is a function `f(req::HTTP.Request) -> HTTP.Response`, run with
`serve!`. A stream handler is a function `f(stream::HTTP.Stream)`, run with
`listen!`. Middleware used with stream handlers must take and return stream
handlers.

### `HTTP.Handlers.Middleware` — Type

    Middleware

The name of the middleware interface. Nothing subtypes or dispatches on it.
Middleware is a function that takes a `Handler` and returns a new one.

### `HTTP.Handlers.Router` — Type

    HTTP.Router([_404], [_405], [middleware])

A handler that calls the handler `register!`ed for the request's method
and path. `_404` handles a path with no route, and `_405` a path whose routes
do not accept the method; by default they return empty 404 and 405 responses.
`middleware`, if given, wraps each handler as it is registered. A router works
with request handlers (`serve!`) and with stream handlers (`listen!`).

A route path is made of segments:

- exact segments, such as `/users`
- variables, such as `/users/{id}`
- variables with a regular expression, such as `/files/{name:\w+}`
- `*`, which matches any one segment
- `**` at the end, which matches the rest of the path

A handler reads the matched route with `getroute` and its variables with
`getparams` and `getparam`.

### `HTTP.Handlers.Node` — Type

    Node

Internal trie node used by `Router` to store exact, wildcard, and parameterized
path segments.

### `HTTP.Handlers.register!` — Function

    register!(router, method, path, handler) -> Nothing
    register!(router, path, handler) -> Nothing
    register!(handler, router, method, path) -> Nothing
    register!(handler, router, path) -> Nothing

Add a route to `router`: requests with `method` and a path matching `path` go to
`handler`. Without `method`, the route accepts every method. See
`Router` for the path syntax.

The handler-first forms allow `do` blocks:

```julia
HTTP.register!(router, "GET", "/users/{id}") do req
    return HTTP.Response(200; body = HTTP.getparam(req, "id"))
end
```

### `HTTP.Handlers.getroute` — Function

    HTTP.getroute(req) -> Union{Nothing, String}

Return the registered path, such as `"/users/{id}"`, of the route that matched
`req`, or `nothing`.

### `HTTP.Handlers.getparams` — Function

    HTTP.getparams(req) -> Union{Nothing, Dict{String, String}}

Return the path variables of the route that matched `req`, or `nothing` when no
route matched or it has no variables.

### `HTTP.Handlers.getparam` — Function

    HTTP.getparam(req, name, default=nothing)

Return the path variable `name` of the route that matched `req`, or `default`.

### `HTTP.Handlers.getcookies` — Function

    HTTP.getcookies(req) -> Vector{Cookie}

Return the cookies in the `Cookie` header of `req`.

### `HTTP.Handlers.handlertimeout` — Function

    handlertimeout(timeout_s; status=503, body="handler timed out", content_type="text/plain; charset=utf-8")
        -> middleware

Return middleware that answers with `status`, `body`, and `content_type` when a
request handler takes longer than `timeout_s` seconds. The handler runs with a
child `RequestContext` whose deadline is the earlier of the timeout and
the request's own deadline. At the timeout that context is canceled, but the
handler keeps running until it returns or checks the context. Only request
handlers are supported.

### `HTTP.Handlers.logging_middleware` — Function

    logging_middleware(handler; logger=nothing, level=Logging.Info) -> handler

Wrap `handler` so that each request it handles logs one record, an access log.

The message reads like `GET /users/1 200 0.412ms`. The record has the request
`method` and `target`, the response `status`, the handler's time in
`elapsed_ms`, and the response body `length` in bytes when it is known without
reading the body (`nothing` otherwise). Records are in the `:access` log group
and logged at `level`, to `logger` when given and to the current logger
otherwise. When the handler throws, the record is logged at `Logging.Error`
with the exception and the status the server sends, and the exception is
rethrown.

It wraps request handlers and stream handlers. Stream handler records also have
the client's `peer` address from `peeraddr`. For a stream handler, the
middleware finishes the response (`closewrite`) before logging, so a response
that fails then, such as a body shorter than its `Content-Length`, is logged as
that failure.

```julia
server = HTTP.serve!(HTTP.Handlers.logging_middleware(router), "127.0.0.1", 8080)
```

## Server-Sent Events

### `HTTP.SSEEvent` — Type

    SSEEvent(data; event=nothing, id=nothing, retry=nothing)

One server-sent event: what a server writes to an `SSEStream`, and what
the client passes to an `sse_callback`.

Fields:
- `data`: the event data; several `data:` lines are joined with `"\n"`
- `event`: the event type, or `nothing`
- `id`: the last event ID received, or `nothing`
- `retry`: the last reconnection time received, in milliseconds, or `nothing`
- `fields`: the event's fields by name

### `HTTP.SSEStream` — Type

    SSEStream(; max_len=16*1024*1024)

The body of a server-sent event response from `sse_stream`.
`write(stream, event::SSEEvent)` sends an event and `close(stream)` ends the
response. `max_len` limits the size of one event, in bytes.

### `HTTP.sse_stream` — Function

    sse_stream(status=200; max_len=16*1024*1024, kwargs...) -> Response
    sse_stream(f, status; max_len=16*1024*1024, kwargs...) -> Response
    sse_stream(response[, f]) -> SSEStream

Build a server-sent event response for a `serve!` handler to return. It has an
`SSEStream` body and the headers `Content-Type: text/event-stream` and
`Cache-Control: no-cache`. The other keywords are those of
`Response`.

With a function `f`, usually a `do` block as in `sse_stream(200) do stream`,
`f(stream)` runs on its own task and writes `SSEEvent`s to the stream;
the response ends when `f` returns.
Without `f`, write events to `response.body` and close it to end the response.

The `response` forms take a `Response` whose body is already an `SSEStream`,
set its headers, start `f` if given, and return the stream.

---

<!-- Page: https://juliaweb.github.io/HTTP.jl/stable/api/websockets/ -->

# WebSockets API

## Module and Core Types

### `HTTP.WebSockets` — Module

    HTTP.WebSockets

WebSocket clients and servers. `open` connects to a server, and
`listen!` starts one; `upgrade` serves WebSockets from an
`HTTP.listen!` handler. Each connection is a `WebSocket`.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.Conn` — Type

    Conn

Low-level WebSocket codec connection state.

This is primarily useful for advanced integrations that need direct access to
frame-level state. Most client and server code should work with
`WebSocket` instead.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.CloseFrameBody` — Type

    CloseFrameBody(code, reason="")

Structured close payload carrying the WebSocket close status code and optional
UTF-8 reason text.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.WebSocketError` — Type

    WebSocketError

Raised when a WebSocket is closed or breaks the protocol. `err.message` is the
`CloseFrameBody`: codes 1000, 1001, and 1005 mean a normal close.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.WebSocket` — Type

    WebSocket

One WebSocket connection, returned by `open` and passed to the handler
of a WebSocket server. Use `send`, `receive`, `ping`,
`pong`, and `close(ws)`. Iterating over it yields each message until
the peer closes the connection.

## Client Operations

### `HTTP.WebSockets.open` — Function

    open(url; kwargs...) -> WebSocket
    open(f, url; kwargs...)

Connect to the WebSocket server at `url`, a `ws://` or `wss://` URL, and return
the `WebSocket`. With a function `f`, `open` calls `f(ws)`, closes the
connection with status 1000 when `f` returns, and returns the value of `f`.

- `headers`, `query`, `subprotocols`: the handshake's headers, query
  parameters, and offered subprotocols.
- `maxframesize = 16 MiB`, `maxfragmentation = 1024`: the largest incoming
  frame, and the most frames in one message.
- `compress = false`: offer permessage-deflate compression
  ([RFC 7692](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7692)), used when the server
  accepts it.
- `connect_timeout = 30`, `request_timeout`, `response_header_timeout`,
  `read_idle_timeout`, `write_idle_timeout`: handshake timeouts in seconds, as
  for `HTTP.request`. `read_idle_timeout` keeps applying after the handshake:
  if nothing arrives for that long, the connection closes.
- `client`, `proxy`, `redirect`, `redirect_limit`, `redirect_method`,
  `forwardheaders`, `cookies`, `cookiejar`, `require_ssl_verification`: as for
  `HTTP.request`.

    open(io::IO; target="/", host="", headers=[], subprotocols=String[],
         maxframesize=16 MiB, maxfragmentation=1024) -> WebSocket
    open(f, io::IO; kwargs...)

Do the client handshake over `io`, a stream that is already connected, such as
a `TCPSocket` or a TLS stream, instead of connecting to a URL. `target` is the
request path, and `host` the `Host` header, which is left out when empty.
`open` never closes `io`; with `f`, it sends a close frame over `io` when `f`
returns.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.send` — Function

    send(ws, message) -> Int

Send one text or binary message on `ws`.

`message` may be an `AbstractString`, an `AbstractVector{UInt8}`, or an
iterable of chunks. Iterable inputs are sent as one fragmented message and the
returned value is the total payload bytes sent.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.receive` — Function

    receive(ws) -> Union{String, Vector{UInt8}}

Receive the next complete message from `ws`.

Text messages are returned as `String`; binary messages are returned as
`Vector{UInt8}`. Throws `WebSocketError` once the connection has closed.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.ping` — Function

    ping(ws, data=UInt8[]) -> nothing

Send a WebSocket ping control frame with optional payload bytes.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.pong` — Function

    pong(ws, data=UInt8[]) -> nothing

Send a WebSocket pong control frame with optional payload bytes.

## Server Operations

### `HTTP.WebSockets.Server` — Type

    Server(; network="tcp", address="127.0.0.1:0", handler, tls_config=nothing, ...)

WebSocket server handle returned by `listen!` and `serve!`.

Hold onto the returned value so you can inspect its bound address with
`server_addr`, wait on it with `wait(server)`, or stop it with
`forceclose`.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.listen!` — Function

    listen!(handler, host="127.0.0.1", port=8080; kwargs...) -> Server

Start a WebSocket server in the background and return its `Server`.
`handler(ws::WebSocket)` runs for each connection. Port `0`, or
`listenany = true`, picks a free port; `server_addr` returns the
address.

- `tls_config`: a `Reseau.TLS.Config` to serve `wss://`.
- `subprotocols`: the subprotocols the server accepts.
- `check_origin`: a function `(request)` or `(request, origin)` that returns
  `true` to accept a handshake. By default a handshake with an `Origin` header
  is accepted only when the origin's scheme, host, and port match the server.
- `compress = false`: accept permessage-deflate compression
  ([RFC 7692](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7692)) from clients that offer
  it.
- `maxframesize = 16 MiB`, `maxfragmentation = 1024`: the largest incoming
  frame, and the most frames in one message.

WebSocket server tasks use Julia's `:interactive` thread pool. Start Julia with
at least one interactive thread, such as `--threads=4,1`, to isolate server work
from non-yielding tasks on the default pool. Without an interactive thread,
Julia falls back to the default pool.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.listen` — Function

    listen(handler, host="127.0.0.1", port=8080; kwargs...) -> Server

Start a WebSocket server and block until it exits.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.serve!` — Function

`serve!` is another name for `listen!`.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.upgrade` — Function

    upgrade(f, stream::HTTP.Stream; subprotocols=String[], check_origin=nothing,
            maxframesize=16 MiB, maxfragmentation=1024, compress=false)

Answer a WebSocket handshake on an HTTP/1.1 server `stream` and call
`f(ws::WebSocket)`. Use it in an `HTTP.listen!` handler to serve WebSockets and
ordinary HTTP routes from one server. Check the request with
`isupgrade` first, and call `upgrade` before writing to the stream:

```julia
HTTP.listen!("127.0.0.1", 8080) do stream
    if HTTP.WebSockets.isupgrade(stream.message)
        HTTP.WebSockets.upgrade(stream) do ws
            for msg in ws
                HTTP.WebSockets.send(ws, msg)
            end
        end
    else
        HTTP.setstatus(stream, 200)
        HTTP.startwrite(stream)
        write(stream, "ok")
    end
end
```

`upgrade` returns when `f` does, and the connection is then closed. The
keywords work as for `listen!`. A stream on an HTTP/2 connection
throws `WebSocketError`.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.isupgrade` — Function

    isupgrade(message) -> Bool

Return `true` when `message` is a WebSocket upgrade. For a request this checks
for a valid client upgrade handshake — use it to guard `upgrade` inside
an `HTTP.listen!` stream handler. For a response it checks for a `101 Switching
Protocols` handshake response.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.server_addr` — Function

    server_addr(server) -> String

Return the host:port address currently bound by `server`.

### `HTTP.WebSockets.forceclose` — Function

    forceclose(server) -> nothing

Immediately stop accepting new WebSocket connections and close active sessions.
